instruments.name: Covered Call
instruments.summary: Long stock plus a short call on the same shares: the writer is paid a premium today and gives up any gain above the strike, so by put-call parity the payoff shape is the same as a short put at that strike. The decision it turns on is whether the premium received is worth more than the upside above the strike, which needs a view on direction AND on implied versus expected volatility.

pros.text: Generates premium income immediately, which raises the yield on a holding the manager expects to go sideways and monetizes a neutral view without selling the shares.
If the shares are called, the effective sale price is the strike plus the premium, above the strike alone. Own at 50, write the X=55 call for 2, and max profit is (55 - 50) + 2 = 7.
The premium lowers the breakeven to S0 - premium, so a modest decline is absorbed. Own at 50 and write for 2, and the position still breaks even at 48.

Reduces net delta below +1 without disposing of the shares. 1,000 shares against calls on 1,000 shares at delta 0.4 gives net delta +600, so exposure falls with no realisation of the gain at the time of writing and no market impact from a block trade.

The short call leg wins when realized volatility comes in below the implied volatility received, so implied volatility above the manager's own forecast is what puts the writer on the right side of the option trade.
Requires no cash outlay. Unlike a protective put it is funded by the premium received, so it does not drag on return in a flat market.

cons.text: The upside above the strike is forfeited. Max profit is fixed at (X - S0) + premium no matter how far the stock runs, so a strong rally is pure opportunity cost.
It does not protect the downside. The only cushion is the premium, so max loss is S0 - premium and the shares can still fall to near zero. A covered call is income, not insurance.

The payoff is asymmetric: the gain is capped at (X - S0) + premium while a sharp fall still costs almost the whole value of the position. That large downside belongs to the shares rather than to the short call, which improves the outcome by the premium received, but a buy-write still has to be sized as an equity position and never treated as riskless premium.

Short gamma runs the wrong way for the holder. As the stock rises the short call's delta grows and net delta falls toward zero, so gains decelerate into the cap; as the stock falls that delta decays and net delta climbs back toward +1, so full downside exposure returns exactly when it is least wanted.
A rally through the strike means the shares are called away, a sale the holder may not have wanted to make, unless the writer closes or rolls the call up and out at a loss on the option leg.

On a low-basis concentrated holding, assignment realizes the capital gain the holder was deferring. American-style equity calls can also be assigned early, most likely just before an ex-dividend date when the dividend exceeds the call's remaining time value, so the writer can lose both the shares and the dividend sooner than expected.
Needs ongoing management: rolling or closing the short call as expiry nears, plus transaction costs on every option trade, which eat into the premium collected.

whenToRecommend: The client holds a large equity position, expects it to trade flat to slightly higher over the next few months, and has asked for more income from it. On the direction-by-volatility grid that is the bullish plus low-volatility cell: sell puts or write a covered call. Bearish plus low volatility is a covered call too (sell calls, covered), but a genuinely direction-neutral low-volatility view belongs to a short straddle or strangle, not here.
The vignette gives an implied volatility above the manager's own volatility forecast, so options are rich and the manager should be writing rather than buying.
The holder already has a target exit price. Write the call at that strike and assignment delivers the intended sale at strike plus premium.

The manager wants to trim equity delta without selling: a block too large to sell cleanly, or a disposal the client does not want to signal. In a tax-sensitive account this works only with a strike far enough out of the money that assignment is unlikely, because assignment forces the sale.
whenNotTo: The stated concern is downside protection or capital preservation. A covered call provides none. Recommend a protective put for a floor above the strike, a collar if the put premium is the objection (the short call finances the put, paid for with the upside), or a put spread if only the first part of the decline needs covering.
A near-term catalyst could produce a large upward move: earnings, a takeover approach, a regulatory decision. The cap costs real money here, so buy calls or a bull call spread instead.

Implied volatility sits below the manager's own volatility forecast. The options are cheap relative to the move expected, so writing is the wrong side of the trade. Thin premium in absolute terms is a practical annoyance, not the test.
The holding is low-basis and the client cannot accept a taxable sale, because assignment forces one. Use a protective put, or a collar struck so the shares are unlikely to be called.
The view is a large move with no direction. Buy a straddle or strangle. Writing is the wrong side of a long-volatility view.
pitfalls: Writing that the covered call has unlimited downside. The loss is bounded at S0 - premium because the stock stops at zero. Unlimited loss belongs to a naked short call, not a covered one.

Confusing the effective sale price with max profit. Effective sale price if called is X + premium, max profit is (X - S0) + premium, and breakeven is S0 - premium, not the strike. Items that ask you to check a proposal's math turn on exactly this distinction.

Reversing the implied volatility logic. Writing is attractive when expected volatility is BELOW implied volatility, because the options are overpriced. A vignette claiming the strategy works when expected volatility exceeds implied has the direction backwards, and saying so is the mark.
Calling it a hedge, or saying it protects or insures the position. It cushions a decline by the premium and nothing more.

Sign error and scale error on delta. The short call SUBTRACTS delta: net delta = shares - (number of options x call delta). 1,000 shares against calls on 1,000 shares at delta 0.4 is +600, not +1,400. Carry the multiplier: a listed equity contract covers 100 shares, so 20 contracts is 2,000 options on 2,000 shares of cover, which is how the bank's own vignette reads it.

Importing the long-option Greeks into the writer's position. The warning that getting direction right but volatility wrong still loses money through vega and theta is about the investor who BUYS options. The covered-call writer is short vega and short gamma but LONG theta: decay is the income. A writer who gets volatility wrong loses through implied volatility rising on the short call, and through the upside surrendered once the stock runs past the strike, never through time decay.

Treating a covered call and a short put as opposites. By put-call parity the covered call has the same payoff shape as a short put at the same strike: both cap the upside and both bear the downside of owning the stock, and both are SHORT volatility. A vignette that calls either one long volatility, or calls the covered call protective, is wrong, and saying so is the mark.

cues.signal: The vignette states both views: the stock is expected to be range-bound or to drift slightly higher, and volatility is expected to stay low.
cues.implication: That is the bullish plus low-volatility cell, so write calls against the holding or sell puts. It rules out buying calls, which are long vega but short theta so decay works against the buyer, and it rules out a short straddle, which needs a direction-neutral view.

cues.signal: The case gives an implied volatility number alongside the manager's own volatility estimate.
cues.implication: Compare them before anything else. Implied above expected means options are rich, so write. Implied below expected means writing is the wrong side and the proposal should be rejected on that ground.

cues.signal: The client is worried about a decline, cannot lose more than a stated percentage, or wants a floor under the position.
cues.implication: Rules the covered call out as the answer. The premium is a cushion, not a floor. Protective put for full protection above the strike, collar if the put's cost is the stated objection.

cues.signal: The client says they would be content to sell at a particular price, or that price sits just above the current market.
cues.implication: Assignment is the plan rather than a risk. Write at that strike and, if assigned, the effective sale price is the strike plus the premium. If the stock never finishes above the strike, the shares stay and the premium is kept.

cues.signal: A large unrealized gain, a very low cost basis, or an explicitly tax-sensitive account.
cues.implication: Being called away crystallizes the deferred gain. Push the strike further out of the money, or move to a put or a collar structured so the shares stay put.

cues.signal: A pending earnings release, a takeover approach, a trial result, or any binary catalyst.
cues.implication: A large move is plausible, so the upside being sold is worth more than the premium to this holder. Covered call out. Long calls or a bull spread if directional, a straddle if not.

cues.signal: The manager wants to eliminate the equity exposure altogether, or to fix the price at which the shares will be sold.
cues.implication: A covered call only reduces delta partway, to somewhere below +1. Long the asset plus a short forward is the delta-zero position, which is the comparison LOS d asks for, and it fixes the sale price at the forward price, not at today's spot. An outright sale also takes delta to zero but settles at spot now and realises the gain.

cues.signal: No cash is available for the hedge, or the mandate forbids paying a premium.
cues.implication: Rules in structures funded by premium received. A covered call fits where a protective put does not. If protection is also required, a zero-cost collar.

cues.signal: The underlying pays a dividend and the options are American-style listed equity options.
cues.implication: Early assignment is live around the ex-dividend date once the dividend exceeds the call's remaining time value. The writer can lose the shares and the dividend, so flag it in any practical-considerations answer.

instruments.name: Protective Put
instruments.summary: Long the stock plus a long put: a premium buys a contractual floor at the strike while the shares, the dividends and the whole upside stay with the client. The decision it turns on is how much premium to pay for how high a floor, because everything between today's price and the strike is an uninsured first loss.

pros.text: Floors the loss at a known number while leaving the upside open: max loss = (S0 - X) + premium, max profit unlimited, breakeven = S0 + premium. Own at 50, buy the 45 put for 2, and the worst case is 7 no matter how far the stock falls.

Cuts downside risk without selling, so an embedded capital gain stays unrealized and the client keeps the shares, the dividends and the votes. This is why it sits in the concentrated-position toolkit next to the collar.

Net delta stays positive but below +1, because the long put adds negative delta: the client is left bullish with a floor rather than flat. Hold 1,000 shares, buy 1,000 puts at delta -0.3, and net delta is +700.

The premium is the entire cost, paid up front: no variation margin, no margin calls, and no rebalancing. A long put is long gamma, so protection strengthens as the stock falls and survives an overnight gap down that a dynamic hedge would miss.

Strike and tenor are explicit dials on cost versus protection: a lower strike costs fewer premium dollars and leaves a bigger uninsured first loss, a higher strike floors nearer the current price for more premium, and a longer tenor costs more but postpones the roll. Because the floor is contractual rather than estimated, the strike can be solved backwards from the client's stated maximum loss.

cons.text: The premium is a certain cash cost against an uncertain payoff, and it lifts breakeven to S0 + premium. In the 50/45/2 example the stock has to clear 52 before the hedged position makes anything.

With an out-of-the-money put, nothing between the current price and the strike is covered. That (S0 - X) gap is an uninsured first loss the client eats, which is exactly why max loss is (S0 - X) + premium rather than just the premium.

Equity index puts sit on the rich side of the volatility skew: implied volatility is higher at lower strikes than at higher ones, reflecting crash fear and persistent demand for downside protection, and a steep skew signals expensive protection. Name the unit when you say expensive: the downside strikes a hedger wants are the richest on the surface in implied-volatility terms, even though a lower strike still costs fewer dollars of premium.
Protection stops at expiry. Rolling repays the premium at whatever implied volatility prevails then, and a long put is short theta, so holding insurance through a flat market is a steady bleed.

The clean floor is an expiry result, but a pre-expiry floor still exists and is lower and softer. Put-call parity, S + p = c + PV(X), bounds the hedged position's value below at PV(X), and for an American put p >= X - S bounds it at X outright. What is partial before expiry is the offset: put delta sits strictly between -1 and 0, so a modest decline is cushioned rather than matched one for one, and the mark can still slide toward that floor as theta and any fall in implied volatility erode the put.

It hedges the price, not the concentration: the client still owns one stock, and the put raises no cash and pays no income. Monetization, a staged sale, an exchange fund or a charitable vehicle are still the answer when the problem is diversification or liquidity.

whenToRecommend: The IPS or the client states a maximum tolerable loss on the position over a stated horizon, and the manager must deliver a hard floor rather than a cushion.
A low-basis concentrated holding the client will not sell, where the vignette stresses deferring the capital gain and does not ask for cash to be raised.
A known near-term event risk, earnings, litigation, a regulatory decision, with the manager still bullish beyond it and unwilling to surrender the recovery.
The client refuses to cap the upside, which takes the collar and the covered call off the table.
Implied volatility is low or the put skew is flat, so insurance is cheap relative to the risk being hedged.
whenNotTo: The client wants protection at little or no net cost and will give up gains above a strike: that is the collar, often a zero-cost collar.

Income to fund current spending is a stated objective. A put pays nothing out, while the covered call collects the premium. Keep the label straight: a collar struck for a net credit pays a small amount out, and a true zero-cost collar nets to nothing because the call premium received equals the put premium paid.
Only a moderate decline is feared and the premium looks dear: a bear put spread cheapens the protection, accepting that the deep downside is left unhedged.
The exposure is to be removed outright with no upside wanted and no premium paid: short futures or a short forward takes net delta to zero.
Implied volatility has already spiked and the skew is steep, so insurance is being bought at the top. Prefer a collar, a put spread or a futures hedge, and say why.

The real problem is concentration, liquidity or estate planning rather than price: a staged sale, exchange fund, prepaid variable forward or CRT addresses it, and a put leaves the client holding one stock.
pitfalls: Mangling the three numbers. Max loss is (S0 - X) + premium, not S0 - X and not X - premium, and breakeven is S0 + premium, not X + premium. Own at 50, buy the 45 put for 2: max loss 7, breakeven 52.
Putting a figure on the maximum profit. It is unlimited, S_T - S0 - premium, and an answer that caps it loses the mark.

Flipping the sign because the put is in the money. (S0 - X) + premium goes negative only if X > S0 + premium, not merely when X > S0, and no-arbitrage rules that case out for an American put because p >= X - S0. On the KEND exhibit, stock at 56: the 60 put at 7.20 gives 56 - 60 + 7.20 = a loss of 3.20 per share, and the 65 put at 10.50 gives a loss of 1.50, both with the strike above spot. As the strike rises the worst case shrinks but stays a loss, so never write 'maximum loss is negative, so this is a guaranteed gain'.

Getting the delta wrong, or the units. The long put adds negative delta, so net delta falls below +1 but stays positive; the position is not delta neutral, only long stock plus a short forward is. Net delta is the sum of (quantity x delta) in share equivalents, so 500,000 shares hedged with puts on 500,000 shares at delta -0.25 leaves +375,000. Those puts are 5,000 listed contracts of 100 shares, so convert contracts to share equivalents before multiplying or the hedge is out by a factor of 100.

Comparing the premium received on a covered call with the premium paid on a put and calling the covered call the better hedge. The covered call cushions only by the premium received, max loss S0 - premium and breakeven S0 - premium, so owning at 50 and writing a call for 2 breaks even at 48 and still loses 48 if the stock goes to zero. It is a cushion of exactly the premium, not protection against a large decline.

Carrying the index-put sizing formula into a futures question. The number of index puts is (portfolio value x beta) / (index level x multiplier), so a 10,000,000 portfolio at beta 1.2 against a 4,000 index with a 100 multiplier needs 30 puts. The futures hedge ratio is a different formula: N_f = [(beta_target - beta_portfolio) / beta_futures] x [V / (f x multiplier)], where the denominator uses the futures price f rather than the index level, and the target beta need not be zero.

cues.signal: The client names a maximum acceptable loss on the position, for example 15 percent over 12 months.
cues.implication: A hard floor is being demanded, so the put or the collar is in and the covered call is out. Prove the fit: a 50-strike put at 2.20 on a 56 stock gives a worst case of 8.20 per share, 14.6 percent, inside a 15 percent tolerance.

cues.signal: Low cost basis, large embedded gain, and wording like 'without triggering an immediate taxable sale'.
cues.implication: Rules out the outright sale and points at hedging, protective put or collar, or at monetization, an exchange fund or a charitable vehicle if diversification is also wanted. Scope the tax follow-on correctly: under US tax law the constructive-sale rule bites on a structure that removes substantially all risk of loss AND opportunity for gain, which is a tight collar or a deep-in-the-money put against a tight call, not a standalone put that leaves the upside intact.

cues.signal: Wants to keep all the upside, or expects a rebound once a near-term risk passes.
cues.implication: Rules out the covered call and the collar, which both cap. The protective put is the structure that floors the downside and leaves the upside intact.

cues.signal: Needs income or cash flow from the position to fund lifestyle spending.
cues.implication: Argues against a standalone protective put, which is a cash outflow with no income. Steer to the covered call for premium, or the collar when protection is also required.

cues.signal: 'Zero-cost', or does not want to pay a premium.
cues.implication: Eliminates the protective put as presented. Fund the put by writing an upside call: that is the collar, and the price is the capped upside.

cues.signal: Implied volatility is elevated, the put skew is steep, or the quoted puts look rich against the calls.
cues.implication: The protection is being bought at the most expensive part of the surface. Favor a collar, a put spread or a futures hedge, and name the skew as the reason.

cues.signal: The question asks to compare the overlay's delta with long the asset and short a forward on it.
cues.implication: Long stock plus short forward is delta 0, fully hedged with no upside. Both the covered call and the protective put sit between 0 and +1. Which of the two keeps more delta depends on the option deltas, so compute it rather than asserting it.

cues.signal: The vignette prices a call, a put, the stock and a bond on the same strike and expiry, or quotes a protective put against a fiduciary call.
cues.implication: This is a put-call parity question, not a strategy-selection question. S + p = c + PV(X), so the protective put and the fiduciary call are the same exposure. With the protective put at 52 (stock 50 plus put 2) and the fiduciary call at 54 (call 5 plus PV(X) 49), sell the dear side, write the call and borrow PV(X), buy the cheap side, the stock and the put, and bank the 2.

cues.signal: A large single-stock hedge on a mid-cap, or the words 'over the counter', 'bespoke tenor' or 'counterparty'.
cues.implication: Listed single-stock puts may be too illiquid or too short-dated for the size and horizon, pushing the hedge OTC with counterparty risk and a wider spread. If the vignette stresses counterparty concern, stay with listed options.

instruments.name: Collar
instruments.summary: A collar is a long stock position bracketed by a bought lower strike put and a written higher strike call, so the payoff is locked between the two strikes. The decision it turns on is how much upside the holder will surrender in order to stop paying for the protection.

pros.text: Bounds the payoff between the put strike and the call strike, and the call premium pays for the put, so the protection can be struck at zero net cost. On the notes example, long stock at 50 with a 45 put and a 55 call gives max loss 5 and max profit 5.
Hedges a large low basis holding without an immediate taxable sale, so the embedded capital gain stays deferred and the client keeps the shares.

Sits on the cost versus protection spectrum as the compromise answer: a protective put gives full protection above the strike but costs a premium, a collar reduces or eliminates that cost by capping the upside, a put spread cheapens the protection but leaves the deep downside unhedged. Mind the ordering, because a long put spread is always a net debit: it is cheaper than an outright put, not cheaper than a collar.
Leaves a net positive but reduced delta, so the holding stays a dampened long rather than going directionally flat. Useful when the vignette wants risk cut but not exposure removed.

Can be struck for a net credit by selling the call for more than the put costs, which answers an income objective and a protection objective in the same trade. A protective put, always a net debit, cannot do that.

The same structure cuts currency hedging cost: buy an out of the money put on the foreign currency and sell an out of the money call to fund it, known as a risk reversal, with seagull variants shaping the bounded range further.

cons.text: The upside is surrendered above the call strike. Zero cost is not free: the price is every gain beyond the call strike, which is the objective a collar most often fails in an essay.
Risk inside the band is unchanged. The holder takes the full move from the current price down to the put strike and up to the call strike, so a collar is not a flat or riskless position.
It reshapes the payoff but does not reduce the concentration or the embedded gain. Diversifying without a sale needs an exchange fund, not a collar.
The protection ends at expiry, so a need that runs longer means rolling the structure, closing the current options and opening later dated ones, at whatever the market charges then.

Tax rules bite on concentrated positions. Strikes set close enough together to leave little risk of loss and little opportunity for gain can be treated as a constructive sale, realising the gain the hedge was meant to defer. Separately, the hedge stops the holding period clock, so stock not yet held long enough for long term treatment will not ripen while the collar is on. It does not strip long term status from shares already held beyond a year, and inherited shares are long term from the start.

If the stock finishes above the call strike the shares can be called away, realising the gain the collar was meant to defer, unless the call is bought back or rolled at a loss. An American style short call can also be assigned early, typically ahead of a large dividend.

whenToRecommend: The vignette says the client is nervous about a near term fall, will not pay much for protection, and is willing to give up some upside. That three part sentence is the standard setup for a zero cost collar.
A founder or executive holds a large low basis single stock position and refuses to sell because of the embedded gain, but the concentration risk has to be cut now.
The client states a maximum acceptable loss and a limited or zero premium budget at the same time. A protective put satisfies the first and breaks the second.
The client wants income or at least no cash outlay and treats a stated price as full value, which names the call strike for you.
A long foreign currency exposure needs hedging but the premium on a straight option hedge is objected to, and capping favourable currency moves is acceptable. That is a risk reversal, the FX collar.
whenNotTo: The client insists on keeping full upside participation, for example because a bid or a re rating is expected. Pay for a protective put instead.
The objective is to actually eliminate the concentration rather than cushion it. Use a staged sale, an exchange fund, or a charitable vehicle such as a CRT.
The client needs cash now. A collar raises little or nothing. Borrowing against the position or a prepaid variable forward monetizes and defers the tax.

Reaching zero cost would require strikes close to the current price. The retained upside becomes trivial and the structure risks constructive sale treatment, so either buy the put outright, or hold the put at the client's stated loss limit, push the call strike further out, and accept the resulting debit.

The short leg cannot be covered: the shares are already pledged as loan collateral, or the account is not approved or margined for writing options. A protective put needs no short leg. Where the obstacle is instead a blackout window, an insider restriction, or a corporate anti hedging policy, assume no option hedge is permitted, because those rules reach the bought put as well, and go to a non derivative route.
The view is on volatility rather than direction. A collar is a dampened long, not a volatility trade, so a straddle or strangle is the structure.
pitfalls: Getting the net premium sign wrong. Max loss = (S0 minus put strike) + net premium paid, max profit = (call strike minus S0) minus net premium paid, breakeven = S0 + net premium paid. When the call brings in more than the put costs, the net premium paid is negative, so the floor improves and the breakeven falls below S0.
Measuring the maximum profit and loss from the strikes instead of from the initial stock price. The strikes bound the stock price, not the profit and loss.
Writing that a zero cost collar has no cost. State the cost: the gains above the call strike.

Recommending a collar on a concentrated position without the tax paragraph. Constructive sale risk if the band is narrow, the holding period clock stopping for stock not yet held long term, and assignment of the short call forcing the sale are the marks on offer.
Calling the collar delta neutral, or claiming it removes risk. Its delta is positive but reduced, and the full move between the strikes is still the holder's.

cues.signal: Will not sell because of a low cost basis or a large embedded gain
cues.implication: Hedge rather than divest, so a collar or a protective put. Rules out an outright sale as the primary answer and puts the tax discussion on the mark scheme.

cues.signal: Does not want to pay much for protection, wants it self funding, premium neutral, or cash neutral
cues.implication: The put has to be financed by a written call. That is a collar, not a protective put.

cues.signal: Willing to give up gains above a stated price, or treats a stated price as fair or full value
cues.implication: That price is the call strike. Cap the payoff there and quantify the surrendered upside as a percentage of the current price.

cues.signal: Must retain full upside participation, or a takeover bid is anticipated
cues.implication: A collar fails that objective outright. Recommend a protective put and say the premium is the price of keeping the upside.

cues.signal: Strikes sit close to the current price, or the band is described as narrow
cues.implication: Constructive sale risk, because little risk of loss or opportunity for gain is left. Flag it and widen the band before recommending.

cues.signal: A maximum acceptable loss is given as a percentage or a dollar amount per share
cues.implication: Test the floor against it: (S0 minus put strike) plus net premium paid, divided by S0. The answer is met, nearly met, or breached, and you say which.

cues.signal: Shares are pledged against a loan, or the account is not approved or margined for writing options
cues.implication: The short call cannot be covered, so the collar is unavailable. Recommend the protective put, which has no short leg, and price the premium.

cues.signal: A blackout window, an insider trading restriction, or a corporate anti hedging policy
cues.implication: Those rules reach derivatives on the company's own stock, so the bought put is blocked too and a protective put is not the workaround. Go to a non derivative route: a pre cleared staged sale, an exchange fund, or a charitable vehicle.

cues.signal: Wants income, or current spending needs funding from the position
cues.implication: Strike the collar for a net credit by selling the call for more than the put costs. This is a point a protective put cannot score.

cues.signal: Needs liquidity or cash now, not just protection
cues.implication: A collar raises almost nothing. Shift to monetization: borrow against the position or use a prepaid variable forward.

cues.signal: Concerned about counterparty exposure, or the required strikes and maturity are bespoke
cues.implication: Listed options carry minimal counterparty risk, because the clearinghouse stands between the parties, but only standard strikes and shorter maturities. A tailored OTC collar solves the fit and adds bilateral counterparty risk, so say which trade off the vignette prefers.

cues.signal: Downside protection is described as expensive, or a steep volatility skew is mentioned
cues.implication: The skew is why. Zero cost then requires a call nearer the money, so quantify how little upside is left before calling the structure appropriate.

cues.signal: A currency mandate that will not pay a premium and is indifferent to favourable currency moves
cues.implication: Sell the currency forward outright: no premium, and no upside to protect. A collar or risk reversal is the answer only when some favourable move must be retained.

instruments.name: Bull and Bear Spreads
instruments.summary: A vertical spread: buy one option and sell another of the same type, same underlying and same expiry at a different strike. It turns on a single trade, giving up everything beyond the short strike in exchange for a known worst case and a much lower net cost, and the vignette's cost constraint then decides whether you build it with calls or with puts.

pros.text: Both the gain and the loss are bounded. The notes' worked bull call spread (buy X=50 at 4, sell X=55 at 2) caps the gain at 3 and the loss at 2, a cheaper and moderated version of an outright call, and the bear spread is the mirror image.

The worst case is a number you can state before the trade, so the position can be sized exactly and the downside disclosed to the client up front. For a debit spread it is the net premium paid; for a credit spread it is the strike width less the net credit received.
The premium received on the short leg funds part of the long leg, so the outlay is smaller than for the outright option expressing the same view.
The same payoff can be built with calls or with puts, so you can choose the construction that brings in a net credit: bear spread with calls, bull spread with puts.

Written as exchange-traded options, a vertical replaces dealer credit exposure with the clearinghouse, so it survives an IPS that bars OTC counterparty risk where a forward or swap overlay would not. The exposure is mutualised rather than absent, the short leg carries initial and variation margin, and verticals are also written OTC, so the recommendation has to specify listed options.

cons.text: The cap is real and it binds on exactly the side you wanted. Profit stops at the strike difference less the net debit, or at the net credit received for a credit construction, so a move far beyond the short strike earns nothing extra.

Being right on direction is not enough: the position has to clear the breakeven, and the full maximum loss is taken whenever the underlying finishes at or beyond the long leg's strike on the losing side.
Laid over a holding as protection, a put spread cheapens the cover but leaves the deep downside unhedged, because the protection stops at the short strike instead of continuing toward zero.
Two legs mean two bid-ask spreads and two sets of commissions, which can take a large share of a narrow strike width.
Maximum profit arrives only at expiry. Before then the short leg still carries time value, so an in-the-money spread trades below its stated maximum.
An American-style short leg can be assigned early once it is in the money, a short call especially before a dividend, leaving an unintended position in the underlying.

whenToRecommend: The investor names a target price over a stated horizon, so the short strike can be placed at or just beyond that target and the premium beyond it sold rather than bought.
The investor wants to profit from an expected decline but wants the loss limited if the decline does not happen. A bear spread delivers both; a naked short call or a short futures position does not.
The client will not pay an upfront premium, or the vignette says to minimize the cost of establishing the position: build the spread as a net credit, bear with calls or bull with puts.
A mandate, IPS or risk policy requires a maximum loss that is known and capped before the position is opened.
whenNotTo: The objective is to capture the full extent of a large move and the vignette sets no cost limit and no cap on the loss the investor will accept: buy the outright call or put, which keeps the upside the short leg gives away. The adverb alone does not settle this, because a vignette can expect a sharp move and still want a spread.
Bullish but implied volatility is expected to fall, or the objective is income: the selection grid answer is selling puts or writing a covered call, not a bull spread.
The view is on volatility with no direction: a long straddle or strangle for a big move, a short straddle or a butterfly for a narrow range.

The holding has to be protected all the way down, or the client cannot absorb a gap below the short strike: that is a protective put for full cover, because a put spread's protection stops at the short strike.
The move is expected but not immediately, or the view concerns time decay and the volatility term structure: that is a calendar spread, one strike and two expiries.
pitfalls: Applying the debit formula to a credit spread. Max profit = strike difference less net debit, max loss = net debit, holds only when you paid. For a credit construction max profit is the net credit received and max loss is the strike difference less that credit. Check every answer against the identity: max profit plus max loss equals the strike difference.
Assuming a bear spread must use puts. Either spread works with calls or with puts; the strikes set the direction. Bear spread buys the higher strike and sells the lower; bull spread does the reverse.

Reading the adverb instead of the constraint. A vignette that expects a share price to decline sharply can still be a bear spread question. What selects the spread over the outright put is a stated wish to limit the loss if the move does not happen, or to minimize the cost of opening the position, and the selection grid puts the spread in the big-move cell alongside buying calls.

Ignoring the cost constraint in the vignette. Both constructions have the correct payoff shape, so a sentence about avoiding a cash outlay is what decides between them and is usually worth a mark on its own.
Writing unlimited profit for a bull spread or unlimited loss for a bear spread. Every vertical spread is bounded on both sides.

Breakeven errors. A call-based spread breaks even at the lower strike plus the net premium, a put-based spread at the higher strike minus the net premium, and both hold whether you paid or received. Do not assume the midpoint of the two strikes: it coincides with the breakeven only when the net premium happens to be half the width.

Getting the delta mechanism wrong. Net delta is the long leg's delta less the short leg's, so a bull spread is net long and a bear put spread net short, each smaller in magnitude than the long leg taken alone. The reason is the short leg, not the absence of stock: push both legs deep into the money and each delta approaches 1, so the spread's net delta collapses toward zero rather than toward the +1 of the underlying.

Treating a vertical as volatility-neutral or time-neutral. The legs partly offset, but vega and theta peak at the money, so whichever leg sits nearer the money dominates. The net sign can go either way, and a deep in-the-money vertical can be net short vega.

cues.signal: Wants to profit from an expected move but also wants to limit losses if the move does not materialize.
cues.implication: A defined-risk structure is required. Rules out naked short options and outright futures, and points to a spread rather than an outright option once cost is also mentioned.

cues.signal: Would like to minimize the cost of establishing the position, or to avoid a cash outlay.
cues.implication: Choose the credit construction: bear spread using calls, bull spread using puts. Both constructions give the right payoff shape, so this single line decides the answer. It does not make the position free, because the short leg still has to be margined.

cues.signal: The exhibit lists call and put premiums at two strikes for a single expiration.
cues.implication: A vertical spread calculation is coming. Compute the net premium, then strike width less net premium, then breakeven at the lower strike plus the premium for calls or the higher strike minus it for puts.

cues.signal: Expects prices to move in a certain direction but not immediately.
cues.implication: Timing language means a calendar spread, same strike and different expiries, not a vertical spread.

cues.signal: The client already holds a large position in the underlying.
cues.implication: The question is about an overlay, and the choice sits on a cost-versus-protection spectrum: covered call for income, protective put for full cover, collar for cheap bounded cover, put spread for partial low-cost cover. A put spread is a sanctioned answer here, not an excluded one.

cues.signal: Concerned about counterparty credit, or cannot sign OTC documentation.
cues.implication: Rules out forwards, swaps and any dealer-written structure. Exchange-traded options survive, so a listed vertical clears the constraint, but the answer must say listed, because verticals are also written OTC.

cues.signal: Asked to rank strategies by net delta, or which position is delta neutral.
cues.implication: Bull spread net positive and below a single long call, bear put spread net negative, straddle about zero at inception. Never assign a spread a delta of +1.

cues.signal: Given two of max profit, max loss and the strike width, and asked for the third.
cues.implication: Max profit plus max loss equals the difference between the strikes for every vertical spread, whichever option type built it.

instruments.name: Straddle
instruments.summary: A long straddle buys a call and a put at the same at-the-money strike, same expiry and same underlying: delta-neutral at inception, it pays if the underlying ends far enough from the strike in either direction, or if implied volatility rises before expiry. The decision it turns on is whether the move the vignette forecasts clears the breakevens X +/- (c0 + p0), not which way the underlying goes.

pros.text: Direction-neutral at inception. At an at-the-money strike the long call and long put deltas offset, so delta is close to zero and the position pays on a move either way without taking a side.

The recommendation can be tested rather than argued. Breakevens are X +/- (c0 + p0), both computable from the premiums in the exhibit, so the answer reduces to one question: does the forecast move clear them?

Long vega and long gamma. Delta-hedged, it monetizes realized volatility against the implied volatility paid; held unhedged it can still be closed at a gain if implied volatility rises before the underlying moves at all.
The same structure works in FX: a straddle on a currency pair expresses a view on the pair's volatility rather than its direction.

On an underlying with a listed options market both legs are exchange-traded, so the long-volatility view carries no OTC counterparty exposure and nothing to post as the market moves beyond the premium already paid.

cons.text: The dearest of the option-based long-volatility structures. Both legs sit at the money, where time value and vega per option are highest, and a strangle on the same underlying costs less than an at-the-money straddle.
Needs a large move, not just the right direction. The X = 50 straddle costing 6 loses money anywhere between 44 and 56, so a correct but modest move still loses.
Negative theta. It bleeds value every day the underlying sits near the strike, and decay is fastest for at-the-money options as expiry approaches.
Delta does not stay at zero. Gamma is high at the money, so delta swings sharply once a direction asserts itself and an unmanaged straddle quietly becomes a directional position.
Downside profit is capped, not unlimited. The underlying can fall no further than zero, so the best downside outcome is X - (c0 + p0).

It is an inefficient hedge rather than no hedge. Long stock plus a long straddle does floor the downside, but only at X - (c0 + p0), whereas the same strike bought as a plain protective put floors at X - p0 for roughly half the outlay, because the call leg adds nothing to the floor.

whenToRecommend: The manager is neutral on direction but expects a big move or a rise in implied volatility. That is the buy-straddle cell of the direction-by-volatility grid.
The analyst argues realized volatility will exceed implied volatility and offers no view on which way the underlying goes.
A binary catalyst is named (earnings, a trial result, a vote, a policy decision) and the exhibit shows implied volatility still low or in line with its own history.
A currency manager expects a pair to become much more volatile with no directional view and wants the exposure in options rather than forwards.
The question asks for a position that is delta-neutral at inception while still carrying volatility exposure.
whenNotTo: The vignette gives a direction. Bullish plus rising volatility buys calls or a bull call spread; bearish plus rising volatility buys puts or a bear put spread. A straddle spends half the premium on the leg that expires worthless.
The underlying is expected to trade in a narrow range or implied volatility is expected to fall. Write the straddle instead, or buy a long butterfly if the open-ended loss of writing is unacceptable.

Implied volatility is expected to remain unchanged while the near-term and longer-term views differ. The unchanged-volatility, direction-neutral cell of the curriculum's three-way selection grid is the calendar spread, which earns the faster decay of the near-dated leg.

The premium at an already elevated implied volatility pushes the breakevens outside the move the vignette forecasts. Recompute X +/- (c0 + p0) and compare: a high implied volatility is not by itself a reason to decline, and a manager forecasting a further rise can still be keyed into a long straddle. The trade fails only when the forecast move no longer clears the wider breakevens.

The premium budget is the binding constraint. A long strangle at out-of-the-money strikes, for example 25-delta each, buys the same long-volatility view for less, at the cost of needing a bigger move.

The signal is the skew rather than the level of volatility, that is out-of-the-money put implied volatility judged too rich against out-of-the-money call implied volatility. The skew trade is a risk reversal, sell the rich out-of-the-money put and buy the cheap out-of-the-money call, which is net long delta and needs a short in the underlying to isolate the skew. A straddle is a bet on the level, not the shape.
pitfalls: Calling the maximum profit unlimited on both sides. The upside is unlimited, but the downside maximum is X - (c0 + p0) because the underlying cannot fall below zero. This is the classic error on this structure.

Getting the legs wrong. A long straddle is long a call AND long a put at the SAME strike and expiry. Different strikes is a strangle, long call plus short put is a synthetic long forward, and short call plus short put is a short straddle.
Quoting one breakeven. The answer needs both, lower = X - (c0 + p0) and upper = X + (c0 + p0), plus the statement that the range between them produces a loss.
Treating delta-neutral as low risk. Delta is near zero only at inception and gamma is high, so the position does not stay neutral.
Trying to structure it at zero cost. Two long options always mean a net debit paid; the collar is the structure that can be built at zero cost.

Recommending it on the volatility story alone. The marks come from computing the breakevens at the quoted premiums and showing the forecast move clears them, and a straddle whose breakevens lie beyond the forecast move is the wrong answer however good the volatility argument sounds.

cues.signal: Neutral on direction, implied volatility expected to INCREASE.
cues.implication: Buy a straddle or strangle. This is the exact cell of the direction-by-volatility grid. Writing the straddle is the answer only when volatility is expected to DECREASE, so read the volatility verb before answering.

cues.signal: The underlying is expected to stay in a narrow range, or implied volatility is rich and expected to fall.
cues.implication: Write the straddle: short vega and short gamma collect the premium. Expect the same vignette to ask you to flag the asymmetric tail risk, limited premium against large or unlimited loss.

cues.signal: Implied volatility expected to remain UNCHANGED, with a neutral near term and a directional view further out.
cues.implication: Rules out both the long and the short straddle. The unchanged-volatility, neutral cell of the curriculum's three-way selection grid is the calendar spread, selling the near-dated option and buying the longer-dated one at the same strike.

cues.signal: A known catalyst is named and the exhibit shows implied volatility already elevated against its own history.
cues.implication: Do the arithmetic before rejecting it. Recompute the breakevens at the richer premium and compare them with the forecast move: if the forecast still clears them, or the manager expects implied volatility to rise further, a long straddle can still be the keyed answer. If it does not clear them, declining or dropping to a strangle is the answer.

cues.signal: Cost, premium budget or the word cheaper appears next to a long-volatility view.
cues.implication: Strangle, not straddle. Out-of-the-money strikes cut the premium but push the breakevens further out, so the required move is larger.

cues.signal: Deltas are quoted for the legs, for example a 50-delta call plus a 50-delta put, or 25-delta each.
cues.implication: 50-delta means at the money, so that is the straddle and the most expensive version. Equal out-of-the-money deltas such as 25 describe a strangle. The delta label identifies the structure for you.

cues.signal: The exhibit shows out-of-the-money put implied volatility far above out-of-the-money call implied volatility, and the question asks how to exploit it.
cues.implication: A shape trade, not a level trade: the risk reversal sells the rich out-of-the-money put and buys the cheap out-of-the-money call. Two things the answer must say. It is net long delta, so it needs a short in the underlying to isolate the skew, and it requires a view that put implied volatility is too HIGH relative to call implied volatility, since in equity index options a put-rich skew is the normal state rather than a signal. A long straddle or strangle is right here only if the question separately says the overall level of implied volatility will rise.

cues.signal: The client already owns the position, fears a near-term fall and does not want to pay much.
cues.implication: A hedging question, not a volatility question. Protective put, collar or put spread along the cost-versus-protection spectrum. A straddle would floor the position through its put leg, but at a floor dragged down by the call premium, which buys no protection.

cues.signal: The manager wants exposure to realized variance itself and does not want to manage a changing delta or rebalance.
cues.implication: A variance swap, not a straddle. A straddle's volatility exposure decays and drifts as the underlying moves away from the strike, so its payoff depends on the path, not just on how volatile the period turned out to be.

cues.signal: The IPS or mandate bars OTC counterparty exposure, or requires exchange-traded instruments.
cues.implication: Rules out the variance swap and any OTC volatility product. On an underlying with a listed options market the long-volatility view has to be a listed straddle or strangle.

cues.signal: The view is range-bound or falling volatility, but the IPS prohibits writing uncovered options.
cues.implication: Rules out the short straddle and short strangle. The defined-risk way to be short volatility is a long butterfly: maximum loss the net premium paid, best outcome if the underlying finishes at the middle strike.

instruments.name: Strangle
instruments.summary: A strangle buys (or writes) an out-of-the-money call and an out-of-the-money put on the same underlying and expiry, conventionally the same degree out of the money. It is a direction-neutral volatility trade, and it turns on one decision: pay less premium than the at-the-money straddle in exchange for breakevens that sit further apart.

pros.text: Cheaper than the at-the-money straddle for the same long-volatility view, because both legs are out of the money. In the notes' own example the strangle costs 3 (55 call at 1.5 plus 45 put at 1.5) against 6 for the 50-strike straddle.

Direction neutral at inception: the long call's positive delta and the long put's negative delta offset, the same reason the notes give for the straddle being delta neutral at initiation, so the position isolates a view on volatility rather than taking a side. It is long gamma, so once the underlying moves the net delta takes a side and the neutrality has to be re-established.
The long position's loss is capped at the premium paid while the call-side gain is open ended, so the cost is known in advance and easy to size against a stated premium budget or IPS limit.

Long vega: it gains if implied volatility reprices upward even before the underlying moves, so a trader who positions ahead of the repricing can close at a profit rather than wait for the realised move.

Written, it earns the full premium across a band rather than at a single price: a short strangle keeps everything as long as the underlying finishes anywhere between the two strikes, which happens far more often than finishing at one strike.

It expresses a view on the LEVEL of implied against realised volatility directly: long wins if realised volatility exceeds the implied volatility paid, short wins if realised falls short. A plain forward or future on the underlying, or a directional spread, cannot express that view at all.

The structure transfers to currency work unchanged: FX options, strangles among them, are the standard way to trade a view on currency volatility rather than on direction, so the same payoff arithmetic is examinable in both the options reading and the currency reading.

cons.text: It needs a bigger move than the straddle. In the notes' example the strangle only pays beyond 42 or 58, against 44 or 56 for the straddle, so a correct volatility call can still lose money if the move is merely moderate.

The full premium is lost across a BAND, not at a single price. Max loss of 3 applies anywhere from 45 to 55, whereas the straddle surrenders its whole 6 only at the 50 strike exactly, so the strangle is likelier to finish in its total-loss region.

Lower gamma and lower vega per contract than the at-the-money straddle, because both Greeks peak at the money, so the structure bought for its sensitivity to the move and to the repricing has less of each.

Negative theta: a long option loses value with the passage of time wherever the underlying sits, not only while it is between the strikes. The notes' own rule is that a long position whose expected move has not materialised is exited rather than carried into the final weeks.

Short strangles are asymmetric: limited gain (the premium) against large and on the call side unlimited losses if the market moves sharply. The payoff is negatively skewed, the notes' hook is picking up nickels in front of a steamroller, and being short gamma adds a dynamic-hedging cost. Size and monitor it, never treat it as free income.

Cheaper in premium does not mean buying volatility more cheaply. In currency options the smile puts implied volatility HIGHER on both out-of-the-money wings than at the money, so an FX strangle pays a richer volatility than the straddle it replaced.

whenToRecommend: The manager expects a big move in either direction, states no view on direction, and wants the cheaper of the two long-volatility structures.

FX vignette: a trader believes a pair is about to become much more volatile than usual with no view on whether it appreciates or depreciates, and the quotes are given by delta. Buy the 25-delta strangle.
A premium budget or cost constraint is stated and the position must still be long volatility and delta neutral at inception.
The view is that implied volatility itself will reprice upward, and the position will be closed on that repricing rather than held to expiry.

Short side: an income mandate expecting a range-bound market and falling implied volatility, where the writer wants a band of full-premium profit instead of the single point a short straddle gives, and the tail risk can be sized and monitored.
whenNotTo: The brief is protecting an existing equity holding against a drawdown. A strangle is not a hedging structure: the long put leg does floor the downside at its strike, but you also pay for an upside call that protects nothing against the drawdown. Use a protective put for full protection above the strike, or a collar when the cost must be near zero and the upside can be capped.
There is a directional view. Half the premium goes on a leg that will expire worthless. Use a bull or bear spread for defined-risk direction, or an outright call or put.

The expected move may be only moderate, or a strong directional break is the stated expectation. Use the straddle: breakevens of 44 and 56 against the strangle's 42 and 58, and the at-the-money legs carry the full gamma and vega.
The view is on the volatility TERM STRUCTURE rather than the level. Use a calendar spread, which trades implied volatility differences across maturities.
The view is that the underlying settles near one price. Use a long butterfly, which pays near the middle strike and caps the loss at a small net premium.

The exposure wanted is to realised variance itself rather than to the terminal price. Use a variance swap, which pays on realised VARIANCE and is therefore convex in volatility, so it gains more than a linear position when volatility spikes. Long VIX futures also hedge a volatility spike, but their payoff is linear in the VIX level and a long roll in contango is a persistent drag.
The mandate or IPS bars uncovered short option positions. That rules out the short strangle outright, whatever the volatility view, so check the constraint before offering it.
pitfalls: Breakeven arithmetic: use the TOTAL premium of both legs at each breakeven. Upper is call strike plus total premium, lower is put strike minus total premium. Adding only the call premium on the upside loses the mark.
Do not state max loss as a point. For a strangle it is the total premium across the whole band between the strikes, so quote the band: 3, anywhere from 45 to 55.

Equal distance in strike does not mean equal absolute delta, and a skew widens that gap rather than creating it, because the lognormal distribution is already asymmetric under flat volatility. The construction taught is the same degree out of the money; the FX convention quotes the legs by delta, 25-delta against 25-delta. Match on whichever measure the vignette actually gives you.

Do not fight the labels on a delta-quoted table. A 50-delta pair is at the money, so it prices and behaves as the straddle, fuller gamma and vega for a dearer premium, even where an item calls it a 50-delta strangle. The substance is that lower-delta legs are cheaper and need a bigger move.

Never answer short strangle to a rising-volatility prompt. Writing the structure is the low-volatility cell of the selection grid, and a near-the-money short strangle loses precisely when the long-volatility view turns out right: short vega as implied rises, and short gamma into the realised move, with only the collected premium and the time decay on the writer's side.

Do not describe the short strangle's loss as unlimited in both directions. It is open ended on the call side only; the put side is bounded because the underlying stops at zero, so the worst downside loss is the put strike less the premium received.

cues.signal: Expects the underlying or the exchange rate to become much more volatile than usual, with no strong view on direction.
cues.implication: A delta-neutral long volatility position: long straddle or long strangle. It rules out a forward or future on the underlying and any directional spread, all of which are bets on direction. It does not rule out volatility derivatives: a variance swap or long VIX futures is also a long-volatility answer, so check what the question is actually asking you to choose among.

cues.signal: Wants the cheapest way to express the volatility view, or a premium budget or cost constraint is named.
cues.implication: The strangle over the straddle, out-of-the-money strikes quoted at the same delta. The price of the saving is a wider breakeven band, so say so when you recommend it.

cues.signal: The expected move is described as moderate rather than large, or a strong directional break is the stated expectation, or tight breakevens are what the manager wants.
cues.implication: The straddle, not the strangle. A moderate move dies inside the strangle's 42 to 58 band but clears the straddle's 44 to 56, and the at-the-money legs carry the full gamma and vega.

cues.signal: Option quotes are tabulated by DELTA: 15-delta, 25-delta and 50-delta puts and calls.
cues.implication: The 50-delta pair is at the money and prices as the straddle; the lower-delta pairs are the cheap out-of-the-money structures. Under a rising-volatility view, long an equal number of 25-delta puts and calls is the cheap correct answer, and short an equal number of 15-delta puts and calls is the least appropriate answer in the set.

cues.signal: The forecast is that implied volatility will RISE, as distinct from the underlying making a big realised move.
cues.implication: Long vega is the point, and the trade can be closed on the repricing before expiry. Breakeven arithmetic is an expiry-only measure, so do not use it to reject a position the manager will not hold that long.

cues.signal: Range-bound market expected, premium income wanted, or implied volatility described as elevated relative to realised.
cues.implication: Short strangle: the writer wins when realised volatility falls short of the implied volatility received. Always pair the recommendation with the asymmetric tail loss, the negative skew and position sizing, or the answer is incomplete.

cues.signal: The client or the IPS states a hard cap on how much can be lost.
cues.implication: A LONG strangle satisfies it, maximum loss is the premium paid. A short strangle does not, so the constraint alone rules out the short side regardless of the volatility view.

cues.signal: An implied-volatility table where out-of-the-money put IV sits far above out-of-the-money call IV (the equity index skew, crash fear).
cues.implication: The put leg of a symmetric strangle is the rich leg and the call leg is the cheap one. If the vignette is asking how to exploit the skew rather than the level, a risk reversal or a skew-normalisation trade fits better than a strangle.

cues.signal: A short option position is running into the last few weeks before expiry.
cues.implication: Close or roll it. The notes' rule is that short-option positions are closed or rolled before the final weeks to avoid pin risk; the economics are that most of the premium has already been earned while short gamma and assignment uncertainty at either strike peak, so the remaining reward no longer pays for the risk.

instruments.name: Calendar Spread
instruments.summary: A calendar spread sells a near-dated option and buys a longer-dated option of the same type, same strike and same underlying, so the position collects the faster time decay of the short near leg while staying long the higher-vega far leg. It turns on the horizon: the underlying must hold a range until the near expiry while a longer-dated directional view stays alive.

pros.text: Time decay is more pronounced on a short-dated option than on a long-dated one, so net position theta is positive and the spread accrues value while the underlying sits near the strike. In the curriculum example the near SEP 45 call decays at -0.029 per day against the far JAN 45 call at -0.014, and the position, short the fast leg, nets +0.015.
Delta is approximately zero at inception, so it monetizes a flat near-term view without taking a directional bet at that horizon.

Net vega is positive, because the longer-dated leg has the greater vega. Maximum profit comes when the short leg expires worthless with the underlying near the strike and implied volatility then surges, lifting the remaining long option.

It pays the manager to wait: a longer-term bullish or bearish view sits in the far leg while the near leg, expected to expire worthless, funds the quiet weeks before the view plays out. Other short-premium structures also collect near-term decay, but here the long-dated directional leg survives the near expiry.

It expresses a view across maturities rather than on the level of implied versus realized volatility: calendar spreads exploit differences in implied volatility between expirations, while a single-expiry structure such as a straddle can only trade the level. Which maturity is the rich one depends on the shape of the surface, so do not assume the leg sold is the expensive one.
The near-term sale pays for part of the longer-dated option, so a long calendar costs less to establish than buying the far leg outright.

cons.text: There is no closed-form maximum profit. The legs do not expire together, so value at the near expiry depends on what the remaining long option is then worth, which needs an implied volatility assumption. You cannot write strike difference minus net debit the way you can for a money spread.
The leg sold is the one with the highest gamma, so the main way a long calendar loses is the underlying moving too far, too fast, away from the strike. Delta is near zero but gamma is not.
Being net long vega cuts both ways: a decrease in implied volatility hurts a long calendar. Getting the direction and the decay right and the volatility wrong still loses money.

The theta ordering the trade relies on is not universal. For in-the-money calls it reverses, the curriculum's SEP 40 at -0.007 against the OCT 40 at -0.011, so the longer-dated leg decays faster. That removes the premise of the long calendar and can motivate the short version.

The short near leg has to be managed. Pin risk arises if the underlying finishes near the strike at that expiry; early assignment on an American option arises instead when the short leg goes deep in the money, or when an ex-dividend date falls before the near expiry, not when it sits at the money. Either way the near expiry forces an active decision to close or roll.

whenToRecommend: The client holds a longer-term directional view on a name but states the move is not imminent, and expects the shares to stay in a trading range until roughly the near-term expiry.
Implied volatility is low by historical standards and the manager wants a position that gains if volatility normalizes upward while being paid to wait for it.

The near-term outlook is a trading range and implied volatility is expected to be unchanged. That is the cell of the curriculum's selection grid the calendar spread occupies, where neither buying a straddle, which needs a volatility increase, nor writing one, which needs a decrease, fits.
A catalyst is dated after the near-term expiry: the manager wants exposure to it through the far leg and wants the quiet weeks before it funded by the leg sold.
whenNotTo: The expected move lands inside the life of the option sold. Put the trade at that expiry instead: an outright option if the move really is sharp and implied volatility is expected to rise, or a money spread to cut the cost when the direction view is right but the market is not clearly trending. For a decline that is a bear spread, and if the vignette also asks to minimize the cost of establishing the position, the call version, buy the higher strike call and sell the lower strike call, is the one that comes in at a net credit.
A large move is expected but the direction is unknown. Buy a straddle or strangle. A long calendar loses on a big move either way.
Implied volatility is high and expected to fall. Write a straddle or strangle, or run a short (reverse) calendar, since the long calendar is net long vega.
The mandate is downside protection on an existing holding. Use a protective put or a collar: a calendar spread has delta near zero and floors nothing.
The client already owns the shares and wants near-term income with a capped upside. A covered call harvests the same near-dated theta against an asset already held, with no second expiry to manage.
A maximum profit and loss computable at trade date is required for a defined-risk mandate or a risk report. Use a butterfly or a money spread, whose payoffs settle at a single expiry.
pitfalls: Confusing a calendar (time) spread with a money spread. Calendar: same strike, different expirations. Money: same expiration, different strikes. Both are on the same underlying, and the answer choices routinely swap the two.

Accepting the claim that a calendar spread is appropriate only when implied volatility is expected to increase. It is not. Decay on the short leg with the underlying near the strike is enough, and the grid places the calendar spread in the volatility-unchanged cell. Rising implied volatility raises the profit, it is not a precondition.

Reversing the long and short labels. Long calendar: buy the distant option, sell the near-term one. Short or reverse calendar: buy the near-term, sell the distant, and it wants a big move or falling implied volatility.

Calling the position vega-neutral because the two legs offset. They do not cancel: the longer-dated option has the larger vega, so net vega is positive and the long calendar is a long volatility trade.
Naming a directional move, or capture of a dividend paid between the two expirations, as the source of profit. The source is the faster time decay of the shorter-dated leg.

Testing only one half of a calendar spread recommendation. Both halves are graded: whether the horizon of the client's expected move matches a structure that needs near-term stability, and whether any claim made about implied volatility is correct. In the bundled Minkoff item the horizon mismatch is what the essay rubric rewards, while the defect inside her own statement is the implied-volatility claim, and her description of direction and timing is marked correct.

cues.signal: The manager expects the price to move in a certain direction but not immediately, and expects a trading range in the meantime.
cues.implication: Rules the calendar spread in. A longer-term directional outlook combined with a near-term neutral outlook is exactly the structure's premise, and the shorter-lived option is expected to expire worthless.

cues.signal: The client expects a sharp decline over the next month, and the exhibit quotes only that month's expiry.
cues.implication: Rules the calendar spread out twice over. The move lands inside the life of the option sold, so the near-term stability the structure needs fails, and with a single maturity quoted there is no second expiry to trade. The fit is a bear spread at that expiry, built with calls for a net credit when the client also wants to minimize the cost of establishing the position.

cues.signal: Someone states a calendar spread is appropriate only when implied volatility is expected to increase.
cues.implication: Mark the claim incorrect. The long calendar is long vega and does benefit from a rise, but it can profit on time decay alone with the underlying near the strike and implied volatility unchanged.

cues.signal: Implied volatility is described as low relative to its own history and the underlying is expected to hold a trading range until the near expiry.
cues.implication: Favors a long calendar: that is the market the curriculum says the structure is typically implemented in. A later rise in the level lifts the profit through positive vega but is not required. An exhibit showing near-dated implied volatility above longer-dated is not the same signal, because an inverted surface usually means the market is pricing a near-term move, which is the condition that breaks this trade.

cues.signal: Both legs share a strike and the expiration months differ.
cues.implication: That is a calendar spread. If instead one expiry is shown with two strikes, the structure is a bull or bear money spread and the calendar answer is a distractor.

cues.signal: An earnings release, policy meeting or other catalyst is dated before the near-term expiry.
cues.implication: Breaks the near-term stability a long calendar needs. The gamma risk sits in the short leg, so the move hits before the decay is collected. A catalyst dated between the two expiries is the favorable case.

cues.signal: The options under discussion are in the money rather than at the money, and the exhibit gives a theta for each expiry.
cues.implication: Check the theta ordering before asserting positive net theta. For in-the-money calls the curriculum's ordering reverses and the longer-dated leg decays faster, which removes the long calendar's premise and points to the short version.

cues.signal: The investor wants to profit from a directional view, to limit losses if it fails, and to minimize the cost of establishing the position.
cues.implication: That triple does not select a calendar spread; in the bundled item it selects a bear spread built with calls. The cost clause is the discriminator: a bear spread can be built with calls for a net credit or with puts for a net debit, and minimizing the establishment cost picks the credit version.

instruments.name: Butterfly
instruments.summary: Four contracts across three equally spaced strikes at one expiry: buy one low strike call, sell two middle strike calls, buy one high strike call, paying most if the underlying finishes at the middle strike with loss capped at the net debit. The decision it turns on is whether you want a short volatility position with a hard loss cap. The same word separately names the fixed income curve trade on curvature, which wants movement rather than stillness.

pros.text: Expresses a low volatility view, that the underlying finishes near the middle strike, with risk capped: max profit occurs at the middle strike and max loss is the small net premium paid. A short straddle or short strangle expresses the same neutral view with open ended loss.

All three payoff numbers are fixed at the trade date and fall out of the bull spread plus bear spread decomposition: max profit = (middle strike minus lower strike) minus the net premium, max loss = the net premium, breakevens = lower strike plus the premium and upper strike minus the premium. The formulas assume equally spaced strikes and a single expiry.

The net debit is small and is the entire capital at risk, so margin sits far below what writing naked options for the same neutral view requires. That is what lets a mandate which bars uncovered writing take a short volatility position at all.

Centred on the current price it starts close to delta neutral, so it takes a volatility view without a direction bet. The strikes then do the targeting: the body on a specific forecast, the wings at the edges of the plausible range.

It can be built entirely from calls or entirely from puts with the same payoff, so the manager uses whichever side of the strike chain is more liquid. It also decomposes into a bull spread plus a bear spread, which is the fastest way to derive the payoff under exam pressure.

In fixed income the same name denotes a curvature trade rather than a volatility one: long the wings and short the body profits if curvature increases, and the trade can be built duration neutral so total duration still matches the benchmark and no level bet is taken.

cons.text: The maximum profit occurs at one single point, the middle strike exactly. The payoff peak is a spike, not a plateau, so the realized result is normally well below the maximum even when the view is right.

The full value only appears at expiry, and the legs that have to decay are the two short middle strike calls: with the underlying sitting on the body they are at the money and carry the largest time value of any leg, which is a liability against the position. The long wings' time value works the other way and adds to the value. So the position can show little gain with spot on the body, which makes it a poor fit for a manager who needs the gain inside the reporting period.

Four contracts across three strikes means three bid-ask spreads to cross, with the body crossed at double size, plus per contract commissions, all against a small maximum profit. A trade that looks attractive on mid prices can be poor once execution is counted.

The profit is capped and the whole premium is lost on any finish at or beyond either wing, so it pays nothing in the tail it is betting against. It is a short volatility position with a limited payout, not a cheap way to hold optionality.
It protects nothing. On its own it puts no floor under an existing holding, caps no portfolio drawdown and hedges no liability. A protective put or a collar does that job.

The fixed income version depends on convexity that only pays if volatility materializes, and a duration neutral curve trade is still exposed to the curve moving in a non-parallel way the key rate tilt did not anticipate.

whenToRecommend: The vignette gives a neutral direction view plus a falling or over priced volatility view, for example the manager expects the index to stay in a range through expiry and thinks implied volatility sits above likely realized volatility.

The mandate or IPS forbids uncovered option writing, or caps loss at the premium paid, and the manager still wants to monetize a range bound view. That three part combination, neutral direction plus short volatility plus a loss cap, is the discriminating one: it rules out the short straddle and short strangle and leaves the butterfly.
The manager has a specific price target and a date, so the body can sit on the target and the wings at the edges of the plausible range, with capital at risk known in advance.

A fixed income manager expects curvature to increase, the belly cheapening relative to the wings: go long the wings and short the body, built duration neutral by tilting key rate durations while keeping their sum equal to the benchmark duration.

A fixed income manager expects curvature to decrease, the belly outperforming the wings: that is the opposite leg arrangement, long the body and short the wings, which is the bullet side of the trade.
whenNotTo: The view is a large move of uncertain direction, or a dated event such as earnings, an election or a central bank decision sits before expiry. Use a long straddle, or a long strangle if the premium must be smaller. A long butterfly loses its whole premium on exactly the outcome being predicted.

The view is directional. Use a bull or bear spread for a moderate move with defined risk, or a long call for an uncapped payoff. Note that a long put is not the uncapped mirror of a long call: its gain is capped at the strike less the premium, because the underlying cannot fall below zero.
The job is protecting an existing holding or capping portfolio downside. Use a protective put, or a collar if the put must be financed by giving up upside.

The manager wants to size volatility exposure precisely, or wants exposure that does not depend on where the underlying finishes. Use a variance swap: it pays variance notional times (realized variance minus strike variance), so it settles on the realized path regardless of the terminal level and gives constant exposure per unit of variance. The butterfly's volatility exposure instead depends on where spot sits relative to the strikes.

The option chain is thin, the bid-ask is wide, or there are no equally spaced strikes around the target. Execution cost across four contracts will exceed a small maximum profit, so prefer a one or two leg structure, with the caveat that a short strangle or a single short option reintroduces open ended loss and so is unavailable under a loss cap. A covered call is not the substitute here: it requires already owning the underlying, its loss is the holding's own downside less the premium, and it is a mildly bullish income view rather than a range view.

The manager wants a near neutral position that gains if implied volatility rises rather than falls. Use a calendar spread, which harvests the faster decay of the short near term leg and is long vega, where the butterfly is short volatility around the body.
