pitfalls: Confusing the two butterflies. In a derivatives vignette it is the three strike option spread, a short volatility position. In a fixed income vignette it is either the curve trade or the curve movement itself. Check which reading the question sits in before answering.

Getting the appetite for movement backwards between them. The option butterfly wants the price to sit still. The curve butterfly, long the wings and short the body, wants the curve's shape to change. The identical words carry opposite views.

Mixing up the positive and negative butterfly labels, which run opposite to intuition because of the inverse price-yield relationship. Butterfly spread = minus the short yield, plus twice the medium yield, minus the long yield. A NEGATIVE butterfly means that spread INCREASES, the belly yield rising relative to the wings, and the position is short the body and long the wings. A POSITIVE butterfly means the spread DECREASES and the position is long the body and short the wings. Safest practice in the exam is to name the legs rather than trust the label.
Using the wrong width in the max profit formula. It is (middle strike minus lower strike) minus the net premium, not the full wing to wing distance, and the formula assumes equally spaced strikes.
Quoting the maximum profit when the question asks for the likely or expected outcome. The maximum requires the underlying to finish exactly at the middle strike.
Forgetting that a long butterfly is a net debit, so the maximum loss is that debit and it is incurred on any finish at or beyond either wing, not only on a catastrophic move.

In the fixed income version, taking the curvature bet without matching total duration, which leaves an unintended level bet. Tilt the key rate durations while keeping their sum equal to the benchmark duration, then evaluate with scenario analysis across parallel, steepener, flattener, butterfly and unchanged cases.

cues.signal: The manager expects the underlying to trade in a narrow range through expiry, or says implied volatility looks high relative to what will be realized.
cues.implication: A short volatility structure is wanted. Combined with any cap on loss, that rules in a long butterfly and rules out a short straddle or short strangle.

cues.signal: The mandate prohibits uncovered or naked option writing, or the IPS caps loss at the premium paid.
cues.implication: Rules out short straddles, short strangles and naked calls, whose loss is open ended. A long butterfly delivers the same neutral, short volatility view with loss capped at the net debit.

cues.signal: A single target price is named, plus limited capital or a small option budget.
cues.implication: Rules in a long butterfly centred on the target: the body sits on the forecast, the wings bracket the range, and the debit is the entire exposure.

cues.signal: A large move is expected but the direction is unknown, or a binding event sits before expiry.
cues.implication: Rules out a long butterfly, which pays nothing beyond the wings. Rules in a long straddle, or a long strangle for a smaller premium and wider breakevens. A loss limit does not change that answer, because a long straddle's loss is already capped at the total premium paid.

cues.signal: The vignette mentions key rate durations, duration neutrality, 2s/10s/30s tenors, or the butterfly spread.
cues.implication: This is the fixed income butterfly, not the option spread. Answer with a key rate duration tilt whose sum still equals the benchmark duration.

cues.signal: The curve is expected to bend with the belly cheapening relative to the wings, or the vignette names a negative butterfly.
cues.implication: The butterfly spread is increasing. Go long the wings and short the body, the barbell side. The opposite wording, a positive butterfly or the belly outperforming, means long the body and short the wings, the bullet side.

cues.signal: An immunized or liability matched portfolio is matched only on overall duration, and the question raises a twist or butterfly move.
cues.implication: Structural risk. Total duration matching is not enough and immunization is imperfect, worse with higher dispersion and convexity, so the answer is key rate durations plus the dispersion and convexity conditions.

cues.signal: Thin option volume, wide bid-ask, or strikes not available at equal spacing around the target.
cues.implication: Execution cost across four contracts will swamp a small maximum profit. Prefer a one or two leg structure, or express the view in the more liquid of the call or put chain, remembering that a single short option reintroduces uncapped loss.

instruments.name: Interest Rate Swap
instruments.summary: An over-the-counter contract to exchange a fixed rate for a floating reference rate on an agreed notional for an agreed tenor, with no principal exchanged and zero value at initiation. The single decision it turns on is direction: receive-fixed adds duration, pay-fixed removes it.

pros.text: The notional needed to hit a duration target is NP = [(D_target minus D_portfolio) times V_portfolio] / D_swap, so one trade retargets rate exposure without trading bonds: NP = [(6 minus 4) times 100,000,000] / 7 = 28.6 million notional, entered receive-fixed to lift duration from 4 to 6.

It hedges the interest-rate sensitivity of the liabilities, which is what drives funded-status volatility in a DB plan, so it is the core liability-driven investing tool alongside long bonds and bond futures.

Capital efficient. A receive-fixed overlay raises asset BPV toward the liability BPV without the cash to buy the long bonds: a plan with 450 million of assets against 500 million of liabilities (BPV 900,000) can lift asset BPV toward that 900,000 without holding the full 500 million in bonds.
Over-the-counter and customizable to the exact tenor and notional, so it fits a precise or longer-horizon duration target such as matching a pension's liability duration.
No cheapest-to-deliver bond and no conversion factor, so the delivery-option and CTD basis complications of bond futures do not arise. A swap prices off the swap curve.
A single maturity, so a multi-year hedge needs no quarterly roll and carries no uncertain roll cost.

A swap has zero value at initiation and costs no up-front premium, unlike a purchased receiver swaption. Where rates are expected to stay low, the receive-fixed swap is the keyed default derivative for closing a negative duration gap.

cons.text: Counterparty credit exposure and lower liquidity than exchange-traded bond futures, where a clearinghouse stands between the parties. Central clearing and collateral mitigate a swap's counterparty risk; they do not remove it, and the word 'bilateral' belongs to forwards rather than to a cleared swap.

It does not eliminate basis risk. When a derivative sets the BPV, the swap may not track the liability's discount rate exactly, and liabilities are often discounted at a credit or corporate rate while the hedging assets move with risk-free or swap rates, so assets and liabilities diverge even when durations match.

Operational and regulatory setup: an ISDA agreement, initial margin, ongoing variation margin, and clearing requirements under rules such as Dodd-Frank. Even a fully hedged overlay needs a cash buffer to meet margin calls.

It changes duration only. It does not hedge credit spread, does not close a funding deficit, and a portfolio matched on overall duration alone is still exposed to steepening, flattening and butterfly moves.
The payoff is linear and two-sided: a receive-fixed position loses value as rates rise and the loss is not capped. A purchased receiver swaption caps the downside at the premium instead.
Harder and costlier to exit or resize than futures. Unwinding means a negotiated termination at mark-to-market or an offsetting swap, not a click in a deep listed market.

Collateral exhaustion risk. A large notional hedge generates big daily collateral and margin flows, so collateral availability itself limits the feasible hedging ratio, which is one reason partial hedges are common in practice.

whenToRecommend: A DB plan or insurer has a negative duration gap (liability BPV above asset BPV) and the sponsor will not raise the bond allocation: enter receive-fixed, sized from Asset BPV + [NP times Swap BPV / 100] = Liability BPV, then multiply that notional by the hedging ratio if the vignette hedges less than 100 percent.
The duration change is large, lasting, or tied to a specific liability tenor, so a standardized quarterly futures contract would have to be rolled many times.
A corporate issuer has floating-rate debt and wants a known all-in fixed cost: pay-fixed converts the floating-rate note to synthetic fixed. Issuing fixed and receiving fixed does the reverse.
The plan is fully invested with little spare cash and still needs more liability-hedging duration, so a capital-efficient overlay beats funding a bond purchase. Hold a liquidity buffer for margin.

An issuer has a borrowing scheduled for a future date and wants today's rate locked against a rise: a forward-starting PAY-fixed swap. Name the direction, and note that the mirror case, a manager with cash to invest soon, is keyed to a pre-investment hedge using long bond futures rather than a swap.
The mandate allows active management of the hedging ratio within a range and the manager expects rates to fall, which favours the linear receive-fixed swap over a premium-paying option.
whenNotTo: The vignette flags counterparty credit exposure, no ISDA in place, or a committee that will not take OTC credit risk: use exchange-traded bond futures, where a clearinghouse stands between the parties and counterparty risk is minimal.
The duration tilt is tactical, a few months, and will be reversed: bond futures are more liquid and easier to unwind.

The client wants the gain if rates fall but will accept no loss if rates rise: only a purchased receiver swaption does that, and the premium is the stated cost. Do not offer a swaption collar here, because the written payer swaption is exercised against you once rates rise above its strike and puts the rates-rise loss back.
The exposure involves two currencies, including principal: a cross-currency swap exchanges interest and usually principal in both currencies, which a single-currency interest rate swap does not do.
The need is index or credit exposure rather than rate exposure: a total return swap delivers the reference index total return with little capital.
Near-term liabilities are known in amount and date and reinvestment risk is the concern: cash-flow matching with actual bonds removes rate and reinvestment risk, which a swap overlay cannot.
pitfalls: Reversing the direction. Receive-fixed ADDS duration (long a fixed-rate bond, short a floater), pay-fixed REDUCES it. Watch the wording: a 'fixed-rate payer' is paying fixed, so duration falls.

Trusting the sign instead of the words in NP = [(D_target minus D_portfolio) times V] / D_swap. Settle the convention first: quote D_swap as the receive-fixed swap's duration, a positive number, and then a positive NP means receive-fixed while a negative NP means pay-fixed on the absolute notional. A pay-fixed position's own modified duration is negative, so plugging that in flips the sign of the answer without changing the trade. State the direction in words either way.

Picking the wrong notional formula. Use NP = [(D_target minus D_portfolio) times V] / D_swap when the vignette gives portfolio and target DURATIONS, and Asset BPV + [NP times Swap BPV / 100] = Liability BPV when it gives asset and liability BPVs. Two classic slips in the BPV form: omitting the division by 100 (swap BPV is quoted per 100 of notional, futures BPV per contract), and solving for the full-hedge notional then forgetting to scale it by the hedging ratio.

Writing that a swap is exchange-traded, or that notional principal changes hands at inception and maturity. A single-currency interest rate swap is over-the-counter and exchanges no principal, only the net interest.
Claiming the swap eliminates basis risk. It removes cheapest-to-deliver basis, not the spread risk between the swap curve and the bonds or liability discount curve.

Answering a 'swaps are superior to futures' claim uncritically. Marks come from validating each true element on both sides (for swaps: precise duration matching, no CTD basis, no quarterly roll; for futures: less operational setup and minimal counterparty risk through the clearinghouse) and then naming what was omitted: swap-curve basis risk against a corporate liability discount curve, futures liquidity, clearing requirements, variation margin plus initial margin, and hedge accounting treatment. The usual conclusion is that both are used.

Forgetting the margin cash. Initial and variation margin on a cleared swap mean a plan that is fully invested must still hold liquidity, and a plan already short of assets cannot assume the overlay is free.

cues.signal: Liability BPV exceeds asset BPV and the sponsor will not increase the fixed-income allocation
cues.implication: A receive-fixed overlay, sized by Asset BPV + [NP times Swap BPV / 100] = Liability BPV and then scaled by the stated hedging ratio if the vignette closes only part of the gap. Buying long bonds is ruled out by the stated constraint, not by the economics, so say so explicitly.

cues.signal: The horizon is several years, or the duration target is pinned to a liability tenor such as 30 years
cues.implication: Swap over futures: exact tenor and notional, no quarterly roll, no CTD. Futures would be rolled repeatedly at uncertain cost.

cues.signal: The committee is uneasy about counterparty exposure, or there is no ISDA agreement
cues.implication: Points away from OTC swaps and forwards and toward exchange-traded bond futures with central clearing and daily margin. Clearing and collateral reduce a swap's counterparty risk without removing it, so a stated IPS or committee constraint still decides the answer.

cues.signal: The tilt is explicitly short term, three to six months, and will be reversed
cues.implication: Futures, not a swap. Liquidity and ease of unwinding dominate customization at that horizon.

cues.signal: The plan wants the gain if rates fall but will accept no loss if rates rise
cues.implication: A purchased receiver swaption, not a linear swap, with the premium as the stated cost. A swaption collar does not satisfy this condition, because the written payer swaption is exercised against the plan when rates rise above its strike.

cues.signal: The vignette states the manager's view on future rates before asking which hedging derivative to use
cues.implication: Apply the keyed rule: rates expected to be low, the receive-fixed swap is the preferred derivative; rates expected to go up, the purchased receiver swaption becomes attractive; rates projected to reach a threshold that depends on option costs and strike rates, the swaption collar becomes the favoured choice. Note that the swap is the instrument with no premium, so a sponsor objecting to an up-front premium points TO the swap, not away from it.

cues.signal: Liabilities are discounted at high-grade or AA corporate yields while the hedge is a swap
cues.implication: Declare swap-curve basis risk. Matching BPV does not make the hedge exact, because the two curves can move apart.

cues.signal: The portfolio is fully invested with no cash, or the plan is underfunded
cues.implication: Capital efficiency is the argument for the overlay, and the liquidity buffer for variation margin is the required caveat. Both belong in the answer, and a funding deficit is closed by a return-seeking sleeve, not by a larger hedge.

cues.signal: A curve steepening or flattening view sits alongside an existing LDI hedge
cues.implication: One swap gives level exposure only, so use a two-leg trade, DV01-neutral and sized modestly as an overlay on top of the hedge rather than a substitute for it. Name the direction: a steepener is receive-fixed at the short tenor and pay-fixed at the long tenor; a flattener is the reverse, pay-fixed short and receive-fixed long. Getting the direction backwards scores zero.

cues.signal: The firm has issued floating-rate debt and wants budget certainty on interest cost
cues.implication: Pay-fixed, receive-floating: the floating-rate note plus the swap is synthetic fixed-rate funding. The all-in cost is the swap fixed rate plus the issue spread.

cues.signal: The mandate sets a hedging-ratio range, for example 25 to 75 percent, rather than a single ratio
cues.implication: This is strategic hedging, so the answer is a ratio choice, not an instrument choice. Expecting lower rates, move to the top of the range with receive-fixed swaps; expecting swap rates to rise, move to the bottom. Performance is measured against holding a preset ratio.

instruments.name: Currency Swap
instruments.summary: A currency swap exchanges principal in two currencies at inception, exchanges interest payments in those two currencies over the life of the contract, and re-exchanges the principal at maturity at the original rate. It turns on one question: is the exposure a fixed, long-dated schedule of interest and principal, which the swap matches exactly, or a market value that drifts, which needs a forward rolled and resized with FX swaps instead?

pros.text: Hedges interest and principal together over a long horizon: the periodic exchanges cover the coupon stream and the final re-exchange covers the redemption amount, which is why cross-currency swaps are the tool for longer-dated interest-and-principal exposures.

Built for foreign-currency debt: it converts both the proceeds and the debt service of a foreign-currency bond issue or loan into the borrower's own currency for the whole life of the borrowing, so the liability and the cash flows that service it sit in the same currency.
One contract covers the whole horizon, so there is nothing to roll and no exposure to whatever forward points prevail at each future expiry.

Changes currency and interest-rate basis at once: legs can be fixed for fixed, fixed for floating or floating for floating, so a borrower can pay fixed at home while receiving floating abroad without a second swap.
OTC and negotiated, so tenor, notional and payment dates are matched to the exposure exactly instead of fitting the exposure to a listed contract.

Opens funding markets the issuer could not otherwise use: it can reach a different investor base or place a larger deal abroad while carrying no foreign-currency exposure. Any funding gain is the new-issue spread or the cross-currency basis, not the lower foreign coupon.

cons.text: Over-the-counter, so it carries counterparty exposure and lower liquidity than a listed contract, and here that exposure runs for years rather than months. Central clearing and collateral mitigate it, they do not remove it.

The notional is fixed at inception, so it cannot track an exposure whose value drifts. A static hedge on a marked-to-market asset goes off target and the notional has to be rebalanced to the current value, which a currency swap cannot do; that is the FX swap's job.

The two legs are in different currencies, so payments are not netted. The full amount changes hands in each currency on every payment date, and again at the principal re-exchange, which concentrates settlement risk at maturity.
Expensive and slow to exit early: unwinding means negotiating a termination payment at market value or entering an offsetting swap, and the offsetting swap leaves residual counterparty exposure.

It does not deliver the cheaper foreign coupon. Covered interest rate parity means a fully hedged foreign position earns the domestic rate, so the all-in cost after swapping lands near home-currency funding. What is left over is the cross-currency basis and the new-issue spread, and the basis can run for you or against you.
It does not touch the credit risk or the local-market price risk of the underlying asset. It converts only the currency and the interest-rate basis it was written on.

whenToRecommend: The firm has a foreign-currency bond or loan outstanding with several years to run and wants the coupon stream and the redemption amount both hedged into its functional currency.

The vignette says the issuer can place a larger deal or reach a better investor base abroad, and management will not carry foreign-currency exposure on the debt. Recommend the swap for the exposure, not for a coupon saving.
The exposure is a liability or a set of contracted cash flows with a known, fixed schedule over a long horizon, not a portfolio whose market value moves.
Both the currency and the interest-rate basis have to change, for example a borrower paying floating in one currency that wants fixed payments in another.
The hedge horizon runs past the liquid part of the forward curve, so rolling short forwards would leave the cost of the hedge hostage to future forward points.
A parent funds a long-lived foreign subsidiary or foreign asset and wants the funding currency matched to those cash flows for the life of the investment.
whenNotTo: Hedging a foreign equity or bond portfolio whose value fluctuates: sell the currency forward instead, and roll and resize with FX swaps, because the hedge notional has to follow the asset value.
Rolling a maturing hedge or moving the hedge ratio: that is an FX swap, a spot transaction plus an offsetting forward, not a currency swap.
A single known payment or receipt a few months out: a currency forward, or currency futures, is enough.

A mandate or IPS bars OTC derivatives outright: the swap is out, and so are forwards and NDFs. Note what is given up, because no listed currency future runs five or ten years and none exchanges principal, so a listed hedge has to be rolled. A stated worry about counterparty credit, on its own, is not a prohibition: answer that one with central clearing, collateral and counterparty limits.
The currency is not freely convertible or deliverable: use non-deliverable forwards, which cash-settle the difference in a convertible currency, because no exchange of principal is possible.
Only the interest-rate exposure needs changing inside one currency: an interest rate swap does it, receive fixed to add duration, pay fixed to cut it.
pitfalls: Calling an FX swap a currency swap, or the reverse. An FX swap is a spot deal plus an offsetting forward with no interim interest exchange, used to roll a hedge and adjust the hedge ratio. A currency swap exchanges interest and principal over time.

Not stating the direction leg by leg. For a hedged foreign-currency bond issue: hand over the foreign-currency proceeds at inception for home currency, then pay home-currency interest and receive foreign-currency interest to service the bond, and reverse the principal at maturity. Derive it from the exposure every time rather than from a mnemonic, because the inception exchange runs the opposite way to the interest legs, and the whole pattern inverts for an investor holding foreign assets instead of owing foreign debt.
Forgetting the principal re-exchange. Hedging only the coupons leaves the redemption amount exposed, and it is the final exchange at the original rate that fixes the principal.
Putting a fixed-notional swap on an asset whose value moves, and never saying that the hedge drifts and would have to be rebalanced. A rising asset becomes under-hedged, a falling one over-hedged.
Claiming the swap captures the cheaper foreign interest rate. The interest differential is embedded in the swap pricing, so the funding gain is the basis or the new-issue spread, not the coupon gap.
Treating the hedge as risk free. It is a multi-year OTC obligation with counterparty exposure, collateral terms, and gross settlement in both currencies.

cues.signal: "Issued a 10-year bond in a foreign currency", or "foreign-currency debt outstanding".
cues.implication: Interest and principal are both exposed for years, which is the cross-currency swap case. A forward hedge would need a separate contract for every coupon plus one for the principal.

cues.signal: "Roll the maturing hedge", or "adjust the hedge ratio as the asset value changes".
cues.implication: That is an FX swap, not a currency swap. The notes' exam focus states it in exactly those words, and naming a currency swap here is the easiest mark to lose on this topic.

cues.signal: "The IPS does not permit OTC derivatives", or "the mandate is limited to exchange-traded instruments".
cues.implication: Rules out the currency swap, and forwards and NDFs with it. Answer with currency futures, but say what is lost: no tenor beyond the liquid listed months, no exact notional or date matching, and no principal exchange, so the hedge has to be rolled repeatedly. A vignette that only says management is concerned about counterparty exposure is not this cue, and calls for clearing, collateral and counterparty limits rather than a different instrument.

cues.signal: "The portfolio has appreciated and the hedge is now off target".
cues.implication: A fixed-notional swap cannot follow it. Sell additional forward to rebalance back to the target hedge ratio.

cues.signal: "We can issue at a lower coupon in that market".
cues.implication: Swap the proceeds and the debt service into the home currency, but say in the answer that covered interest rate parity leaves the all-in cost near home-currency funding, and that the gain, if any, is the new-issue spread or the cross-currency basis rather than the coupon differential.

cues.signal: "Capital controls", "non-convertible", or "not deliverable".
cues.implication: No exchange of principal is possible, so a currency swap is off the table. Use non-deliverable forwards, cash-settled in a convertible currency for the difference between the contracted rate and spot, or a proxy hedge in a correlated currency, accepting basis risk.

cues.signal: "Wants protection but would like to keep the gain if the currency moves our way".
cues.implication: Rules out the swap and the forward: both lock the rate and surrender the favorable move along with the adverse one. Buy the option and pay the premium, a put on the foreign currency for a long foreign-currency exposure. Do not answer with a risk reversal or a seagull, because they fund the premium by capping the favorable side, which is the thing the client asked to keep.

cues.signal: "We hold a foreign government bond, we want the rate view but no currency risk".
cues.implication: Two overlays, not one instrument. Sell the currency forward for the FX exposure and use bond futures for the duration. Currency and rate exposures are managed separately with the right instrument for each.

cues.signal: "Pay floating in one currency but we want fixed payments in another".
cues.implication: One currency swap handles the currency conversion and the interest-rate basis together. A separate interest rate swap is not needed.

cues.signal: "The horizon is uncertain", or "may need to exit within a year".
cues.implication: A multi-year OTC swap is costly to unwind. Shorter rolled instruments or listed futures keep the option to stop cheaply.

instruments.name: Equity Swap
instruments.summary: An equity swap exchanges the return on an equity index or a single stock for a fixed rate, a floating financing rate, the return on another asset class such as a bond index, or another equity return, on an agreed notional and tenor. The decision it turns on is which leg you pay: receive the equity return to add exposure synthetically, pay it to hedge or diversify a holding you will not sell.

pros.text: Reshapes exposure without trading the underlying: receive the index return and pay a financing rate to add equity, or pay the equity return and receive a bond return to switch asset classes, leaving the holdings and the external managers untouched.
Diversifies a concentrated low-basis holding with no taxable sale: pay the return on the stock and receive a diversified index return.

The hedger keeps the shares, so ownership and votes stay with the client while the return is swapped away. Cash settlement is what preserves that, because a physically settled single-stock swap delivers the shares against the notional at termination.

Replication of the referenced index is exact: the counterparty is obligated to deliver the index return, so the equity leg carries no tracking error, unlike an ETF (NAV premium or discount, cash drag, regulatory diversification) or futures (dividend forecast error, interest rate differentials). The receiver's net return is still that index return less financing.

Capital efficient: the notional exposure is delivered against collateral rather than cash, where margin regulation caps an ETF near 2x leverage, so USD 80 million of ETF exposure ties up at least USD 40 million.

No quarterly roll and no exchange-traded margin cycle: one contract can cover the whole horizon, where the roll was the largest single futures cost at 20 bps a year on an upward sloping (contango) curve. Collateral is still posted.

Terms are negotiated, so notional, tenor, reset frequency and the exact index, sector or single name are set to the need, including underlyings with no liquid listed contract or with restricted market access.
Can beat owning the shares outright when holding physical stock carries transaction taxes such as stamp duty, high custodian fees, or costly monitoring of corporate actions.

cons.text: Counterparty credit risk: an equity swap is bilateral and over the counter, so the executive who hedges by swap has replaced stock risk with dealer exposure. Collateral, and central clearing where the contract is eligible for it, mitigate that risk; they do not remove it.
Funding cost dominates the price. In the Exhibit 15 stack the TRS was the dearest unlevered vehicle at 51 bps against the ETF at 35 and futures at 42, and 40 of those 51 bps were funding.

Relatively illiquid and harder to exit than a listed contract: unwinding means negotiating with the dealer or writing an offsetting swap rather than selling into an exchange, and collateral is tied up for the life of the trade.

The payoff is symmetric on both legs and floors nothing. The return receiver pays the negative return plus financing when the index falls, so the loss is not limited to the cash committed; the return payer gives up the holding's appreciation for the whole life of the swap.

If the leg you pay is an index rather than the holding itself, only the systematic component is hedged: stock-specific risk survives, and the hedge carries basis risk if the portfolio's beta to that index is mis-estimated or shifts.
The gain is deferred, not erased: the low-basis shares and the embedded gain stay on the balance sheet, and the structure may face tax or regulatory limits.
Synthetic exposure confers no ownership: the return receiver holds no shares and gets no vote, so a swap cannot satisfy a stewardship or engagement policy.

whenToRecommend: An executive or founder holds a large, low-cost-basis position in employer stock, wants the exposure cut or diversified, and will not trigger the capital gain: pay the stock's total return and receive an index return or a floating rate.
The holding has to be hedged but kept, because the shares are illiquid to trade or because the votes matter: a cash-settled total return payer swap hedges the return and leaves the shares in place.

Replication precision decides the choice once cost is settled: the swap delivers the referenced index return exactly, so prefer it where the mandate penalises tracking error AND the cheaper routes are closed off by funding, leverage or the absence of a listed contract. Exactness on its own does not win the trade.

The exposure is wanted for a year or longer AND the position cannot be fully funded, or no listed contract fits, or a custom notional is needed: the swap avoids the quarterly roll that futures carry. A long horizon on its own does not select the swap, because a fully funded ETF position is cheaper at 35 bps against 51 and also escapes rolls and margin calls.
The plan must shift synthetically between asset classes or sleeves, equities to bonds for instance, without disturbing the underlying managers or realizing gains.

The wanted exposure is an index, sector or single name with no liquid listed contract, or sits in a market where access restrictions, transaction taxes or custody costs make owning the shares impractical.
whenNotTo: The IPS or mandate bars OTC or uncollateralised derivatives: the swap is out, and listed index futures or an ETF reach the same index exposure. A committee that voices counterparty concern without prohibiting OTC can be answered with collateral and, where the contract is eligible, central clearing, but a stated concern is also legitimate grounds to prefer the listed route: the endowment case lists counterparty credit risk as a standing cost of the TRS and picks an exchange-traded vehicle.

The tilt is short term, tactical and quickly reversible: index futures are cheaper to put on and to unwind, 42 bps against the swap's 51. The curriculum draws this line by size and permanence rather than by a fixed number of weeks.
The position is fully funded and unlevered: the ETF was cheapest of the three at 35 bps against the TRS at 51.
The exposure is to be levered: at 4x the ranking flipped and futures were cheapest at 192 bps, against 201 for the TRS and 222.50 for the ETF.
The client wants the exposure plus votes, engagement or stewardship: the return receiver owns no shares, so buy the shares or an index fund.

The objective is to remove the embedded gain rather than defer it: an outright charitable gift of the appreciated shares, or a CRT that sells inside the trust. An exchange fund is not the answer here, because like the swap it diversifies without a sale and so defers the gain at carryover basis rather than eliminating it.
pitfalls: Getting the legs backwards. To add exposure, RECEIVE the equity return and PAY the financing rate. To hedge or diversify a holding, PAY the equity return and receive an index return or a floating rate. The receiver is synthetically long, so a receiver swap written over an existing holding doubles the position instead of hedging it.

Choosing physical settlement when the vignette says the shares are to be kept. A physically settled single-stock swap hands the shares to the receiver against the notional at termination, so a client who wants to keep the holding needs cash settlement.
Netting on the wrong base. The settlement is the return differential times notional: (8% minus 5%) times 20,000,000 equals 600,000. It is not a return applied to a revalued portfolio.

Reaching for the futures beta formula on a swap question. N_f = [(beta_target minus beta_p)/beta_f] x [V/(f x multiplier)] returns a contract count; a swap answer is a notional, a direction on each leg, and a tenor.
Saying the diversification swap is tax free. Say deferred, and add that the structure may face tax or regulatory limits, because the sale has only been postponed.

Leaving the tenor unstated or mismatched. The swap has to run for the period over which protection is wanted, so a vignette expecting five quarters of earnings misses calls for roughly five quarters of cover, not twelve months and not an open-ended hedge. Where the question fixes the tenor in the stem, as the Inwood item does by prefixing every choice 'Buy a one-year', take the tenor from the stem and spend the answer on payer versus receiver and cash versus physical.

cues.signal: The client will not sell because of a large embedded capital gain, or the shares are too illiquid to sell.
cues.implication: Rules out an outright or staged sale. Pay the stock's total return and receive an index return or a floating rate, cash settled so the shares stay put. Choose an option structure instead if the client wants upside: a protective put keeps the whole upside less the premium, a collar keeps it only up to the short call strike and is cheaper or costless because the call funds the put. The swap gives up all of the upside.

cues.signal: The IPS or the mandate prohibits OTC or uncollateralised derivatives.
cues.implication: Rules out the equity swap and every other OTC structure. Answer with exchange-traded index futures or an ETF, which reach the same index exposure. A stated worry about counterparty credit, with no prohibition, is answered by collateral and, where the contract is eligible, central clearing, but it also legitimately supports choosing the listed route instead.

cues.signal: The holding is to be hedged but retained, and the vignette says the shares will not be sold or delivered.
cues.implication: Selects a cash-settled total return payer swap. Physical settlement would deliver the shares against the notional at termination, and a receiver swap would add a second long rather than hedge the first.

cues.signal: Voting, engagement or a stewardship policy is named for exposure the client does not yet own.
cues.implication: Rules out synthetic index exposure. The return receiver holds no shares and gets no vote, so use physical shares or an index fund.

cues.signal: The mandate specifies exact replication or zero tracking error.
cues.implication: Points to the swap on replication: the counterparty is obligated to deliver the index return, while an ETF carries NAV premium or discount and cash drag and futures carry dividend forecast and interest rate differential error. Settle cost first, though, because in the endowment case the swap's exactness was on the table and the ETF still won the fully funded mandate at 35 bps against 51.

cues.signal: The horizon is a year or more, or the committee objects to the daily margin monitoring and quarterly rolls that futures carry.
cues.implication: Moves the answer away from futures, whose roll cost was 20 bps a year on an upward sloping curve. The swap if cash is short, a custom notional is needed or no listed contract fits; the ETF if the position is fully funded, since it is cheaper and has no rolls or margin calls either.

cues.signal: The exposure is to be levered, or cash is constrained.
cues.implication: Rules out the ETF, which margin rules cap near 2x and which was dearest at 4x at 222.50 bps. Between the two synthetic routes futures were cheaper at 192 against 201 with the 20 bps roll already inside that 192, so do not charge the roll again as a tie-breaker. Name the swap only when a custom notional, a missing listed contract, or the operational burden of rolling and monitoring margin decides it, not on cost.

cues.signal: The allocation must change but the external managers and the underlying holdings must not be disturbed.
cues.implication: An overlay answer: pay the equity return and receive the bond return to move equities to bonds, or the reverse. Futures do this too, so what selects the swap is a longer horizon, a custom notional, or no liquid listed contract.

cues.signal: The exposure wanted is a single name, a narrow sector, or a market with restricted access, stamp duty or heavy custody costs.
cues.implication: Owning the physical is penalised, which selects the swap over the SHARES: stamp duty, custody fees and corporate-action monitoring fall on the holder, not on a synthetic. Against futures and an ETF the deciding fact is different, because a fund holder escapes those frictions too; the swap wins only where no listed contract or fund tracks the exposure, which is the single-name case more often than the sector case.

instruments.name: Variance Swap
instruments.summary: An OTC swap that pays the long side the variance notional times (realized variance minus a strike variance fixed at inception), making it a direct, convex position on volatility itself rather than on market direction. The decision it turns on is whether the client needs exposure to volatility, which this pays convexly, or a floor under portfolio value, which it never provides.

pros.text: Convex in volatility. Because it pays on squared volatility it gains more than the linear vega approximation and more than a volatility swap when volatility spikes, which is what a crash hedge has to do.
No roll cost. The strike is fixed at inception for the whole term, so unlike a rolled long VIX futures hedge it does not bleed negative roll yield while the curve sits in contango.
Volatility spikes when equities fall, so a long variance position pays off in the drawdowns when equity diversification is scarcest.

Sized in vega notional, the currency amount earned per volatility point, so the hedge can be quoted and scaled in volatility points. Convert to variance notional before computing anything: variance notional = vega notional / (2 x strike vol).
No premium is paid at inception. The strike is set so the swap is worth zero at the start, so unlike a protective put the hedge needs no cash outlay on day one.
Being OTC, term and strike are negotiated, so the hedge horizon can be matched to the exposure instead of to a listed expiry cycle.

cons.text: It pays on realized variance, not on the portfolio's loss, so it sets no floor on value. Worse, if realized volatility finishes below the strike the long pays the dealer, so a slow orderly decline costs on the equity and on the swap. The long's loss runs up to variance notional x strike variance (realized variance floors at zero), which is 2,500 x 400 = 1,000,000 on a 100,000 vega notional struck at 20%.

The short side is asymmetric: its gain is capped at variance notional x strike variance because realized variance cannot fall below zero, while its loss rises without a corresponding limit as volatility spikes. That is the classic short volatility risk, and the long's profile is the mirror image.

An OTC dealer contract, so the long carries counterparty credit risk for the life of the trade. The listed alternative swaps that risk for a different one: a VIX future is centrally cleared but marked to market daily, so it demands initial and variation margin and a cash buffer even when the hedge is working in economic terms.

The strike tends to be set above the volatility subsequently realized, which is how sellers are paid for supplying the convexity, so the cost of holding long variance permanently shows up as a negative expected payoff rather than as an upfront premium.

Settlement is at expiry on variance realized over an observation window fixed at inception. Variance accrued during a spike is locked into that sum and cannot be given back by later calm days, but the mid-life mark can be: it blends realized variance to date with implied variance for the remaining term, discounted, so a paper gain shrinks as forward implied volatility falls.

whenToRecommend: The vignette asks for a tail hedge against an equity crash and tells you the VIX curve is in contango: the variance swap gains on a volatility spike without paying the roll.
The client wants to hedge or express a view on volatility itself, for example expecting realized volatility to come in above the level implied in option prices, rather than a view on market level.
The hedge must be convex, paying disproportionately more in a severe move than in a mild one, so a linear instrument will not do.
The hedge horizon is specific, say nine months to a known liquidity event, and a listed expiry cycle would force an unwanted roll.
whenNotTo: The IPS bars OTC counterparty exposure or the client requires cleared, exchange traded instruments: use VIX futures or listed index options instead.
The need is protection at a known price level rather than exposure to volatility: a protective put, or a collar if cost matters more than upside, hedges the loss directly.
The payoff must be linear in volatility points, for example to match a stated volatility target or a simple mandate: a volatility swap is the matching instrument.
The client wants premium income: the income trades are covered calls and cash secured puts, not a short variance swap, whose loss rises without limit if volatility spikes.
Volatility is already elevated, so the strike variance is struck off a high implied level and you would be paying for the spike that has already happened.
pitfalls: Dividing by strike volatility instead of 2 x strike volatility. Variance notional = vega notional / (2 x strike vol), so 100,000 with a 20% strike gives 2,500, not 5,000.

Mixing units. Keep volatility in percentage points, the convention the vega notional is quoted in: strike variance 400, realized variance 625, payoff 2,500 x 225 = 562,500. Plugging decimal variances (0.0625 minus 0.04 = 0.0225) into a percentage point variance notional gives 56.25 and understates the answer by a factor of 10,000. Convert the notional and the variance terms together or not at all.
Answering with the linear vega approximation. Vega notional x (realized vol minus strike vol) gives 500,000 where the true payoff is 2,500 x 225 = 562,500, because the swap pays on variance.
Squaring the difference instead of differencing the squares. The payoff uses realized variance minus strike variance, never (realized vol minus strike vol) squared.

Treating a long variance swap as a floor on portfolio value. The curriculum does call it a tail risk hedge against volatility spikes and crashes, so do not deny that framing. The limit is narrower: it pays on realized variance rather than on the loss, and if realized volatility finishes below the strike the long pays out, up to variance notional x strike variance, on top of the equity loss.
Carrying the contango critique across to the swap. Negative roll yield is the VIX futures problem; the variance swap strike is fixed at inception, which is the whole point of the comparison.

Using the expiry payoff to value a swap that is only part way through its term. A live swap is valued as variance notional x PV factor x [(t/T) x realized variance to date + ((T minus t)/T) x implied variance for the remaining term minus strike variance], then signed for the side you hold.

cues.signal: The VIX futures curve is described as being in contango and the mandate is a tail hedge.
cues.implication: A rolled long VIX futures hedge bleeds negative roll yield. The variance swap strike is fixed at inception and never rolls, so it is the preferred tail hedge of the two.

cues.signal: A vega notional and a strike volatility are given, with a realized volatility for the period.
cues.implication: It is a variance swap payoff at expiry. Convert first, variance notional = vega notional / (2 x strike vol), then payoff = variance notional x (realized var minus strike var). Do not stop at the vega approximation.

cues.signal: The vignette gives elapsed time on an existing swap, realized volatility to date, and a new fair strike or implied volatility for the remaining term, plus a discount rate.
cues.implication: That is the mark to market valuation, not the expiry payoff: variance notional x PV factor x [(t/T) x realized variance + ((T minus t)/T) x implied variance minus strike variance]. A negative number is the value to the long, so it is positive by the same amount to the short.

cues.signal: The manager expects realized volatility to exceed the volatility implied in option prices.
cues.implication: That is a variance swap view, because the swap settles on realized variance against a strike fixed at inception. VIX futures settle on the VIX, which is implied volatility, so they can lose on exactly this view. Index futures or a protective put are wrong either way, because this is not a directional view.

cues.signal: The hedge is required to pay disproportionately more in a severe move, or the words convex or non-linear appear.
cues.implication: Variance swap over volatility swap. Variance is squared volatility and therefore convex; a volatility swap pays linearly and gives up that extra payoff in a spike.

cues.signal: The client worries about counterparty risk, or the IPS requires exchange traded or centrally cleared positions.
cues.implication: Rules out the variance swap, which is an OTC dealer contract. Switch the recommendation to VIX futures or listed index options, and note that the cleared route brings a daily variation margin and cash buffer requirement with it.

cues.signal: The portfolio is selling variance, or the question asks you to assess the dealer's side of the trade.
cues.implication: Switch to the short profile: gain capped at variance notional x strike variance because realized variance cannot go below zero, loss rising without limit if volatility spikes. Do not carry that asymmetry onto a long hedge, where it is the mirror image, loss capped and gain uncapped.

cues.signal: The portfolio needs protection against a specific drawdown percentage or a floor on value.
cues.implication: A variance swap does not deliver that. It pays on realized variance, not on the portfolio's loss, so a protective put or collar is the instrument that sets a floor.

instruments.name: Total Return Swap
instruments.summary: An over-the-counter swap in which the total return receiver takes the whole return on a reference equity, commodity or bond index, the cash flows plus any appreciation, and pays MRR plus or minus a predetermined spread, while the payer is compensated by the receiver for any depreciation and for default losses. It turns on one decision: do you want an index's entire total return without owning the assets, or do you want to shed the entire total return of something you refuse to sell? The two sides pay different prices. The receiver's price is the funding leg plus counterparty risk; the payer's price is the forgone appreciation and income plus the dealer's spread and counterparty risk, and she finances nothing because she already owns the asset. Do not memorise one sign for the spread: the bond-index form in the LDI reading is MRR plus a predetermined spread, while the R17 index-swap example has the receiver pay MRR minus the agreed spread.

pros.text: Replication is exact. The counterparty is obligated to deliver the index return, so there is no tracking error, whereas an ETF carries NAV premiums and discounts, cash drag and regulatory diversification limits, and futures carry liquidity and supply-demand effects, dividend forecast error and interest rate differentials.

Capital light. It generates the same economic exposure as an ETF with far less cash committed: an ETF must finance the full notional or use margin, which regulation caps at 50% of account value for a maximum of 2x leverage, so USD80 million of ETF exposure ties up at least USD40 million. Note that futures are capital light on the same argument, so cash efficiency alone does not single out the swap.

Customised and over the counter, so no listed contract need exist. An active futures market is not required for synthetic index exposure, and a TRS can reach assets that are difficult to access directly, such as some high-yield and commercial loan investments.

A TRS on a corporate bond index passes through both the interest rate component and the credit spread component of a liability's discount rate, which is why it is the answer when a plan wants passive exposure to both. Treasury futures and interest rate swaps move the rate component only.

It reshapes exposure with no sale. A holder of a large low-basis position pays the stock's total return, price change plus dividends, and receives either a floating reference rate or a diversified index return, neutralising or diversifying the position while keeping the shares and deferring the tax event rather than triggering a taxable sale.

Preferred to owning the shares when market access is restricted, when taxes on the physical shares that the swap avoids make ownership costly (stamp duty on buying or transferring stock, for example), when custodian fees are high, or when monitoring the position through corporate actions is costly.

cons.text: Counterparty credit risk is added, not swapped away. Performance depends on the dealer, and the total return receiver still compensates the payer for index depreciation and for default losses on the reference portfolio, so on a bond index the receiver keeps the issuers' credit risk and takes the dealer's on top of it.

The dearest of the three implementation vehicles in the QUINCO case's unlevered stack, 51 bps against 42 bps for futures and 35 bps for the ETF, and the total is dominated by the 40 bps funding cost. Those are the case's assumptions, not universal costs.
The contract has a finite life, so a TRS must be rolled. It is not a set and forget holding.

Collateral has to be posted, the contract is bilateral, and it is relatively illiquid next to a listed future or an ETF: exiting early means executing a new offsetting swap for the remainder of the original term or negotiating a termination with the dealer rather than selling in a market, and extending the exposure means renegotiating at expiration. The tenor therefore has to be matched to the period over which the exposure or the protection is wanted. A synthetic receiver holds no shares, so it has no voting rights. Do not push illiquidity too far, though: the LDI notes still call a TRS easy to unwind and suitable for temporary or overlay exposure, so it is not an argument against a short-dated overlay.

It is linear and two sided, not optionality. The payer surrenders the appreciation and the dividends in order to shed the downside, and when the index falls the receiver owes the depreciation on top of the financing leg, so a TRS preserves no upside the way a put or a collar does.

Because the notional is not funded, a TRS can be a source of leverage: the notes list interest rate and total return swaps among the methods of leveraging a fixed-income portfolio, alongside repos and futures. That is a conditional defect, not an automatic one. Unless cash or assets are held against the notional, gains and losses are magnified against the capital actually committed and margin calls can force selling into a falling market.

whenToRecommend: A passive mandate needs exposure to an index with no active futures market, for example a foreign or specialist debt index, so no listed instrument exists to use.

The liability's discount rate contains a credit spread and the plan wants passive exposure that hedges rate and credit together: receive the total return on a corporate bond index, economically a synthetic secured financing.

The portfolio is small and the client doubts that building and maintaining a cell-matched sample is worth his staff's time and the transaction costs, because one swap delivers the whole index; a pooled index fund is an equally acceptable answer.

The exposure is temporary, tactical or an overlay, which is what the notes name the TRS for. Do not extend this to cash or leverage constraints on their own: futures deliver the exposure with as little capital, and on the QUINCO 4x numbers futures are cheaper at 192 bps against the swap's 201.
Tracking error is explicitly unacceptable or the exposure must match the benchmark exactly, and cost is not the binding constraint.

A client holds a large low-basis concentrated position, will not sell, and wants to keep ownership and votes, so she pays the stock's total return and receives a floating reference rate or a diversified index return.
whenNotTo: The IPS bars OTC or uncollateralised derivatives outright, or the vignette makes central clearing or daily settlement a stated requirement. Then use exchange-traded futures or an ETF. A mere worry about counterparty risk is not a disqualifier: answer it with a Credit Support Annex, collateral or clearing.
A fully funded, unlevered overweight where the client values the flexibility to change the view: in the QUINCO case the ETF wins at 35 bps against the TRS at 51 bps.
Leverage is permitted and the test is cost: at 4x the case ranks futures 192 bps, TRS 201 bps and ETF 222.50 bps, so futures win and the TRS is only second.

Only the rate component of the liability needs hedging, for example a duration or BPV adjustment where the discount rate carries no credit spread the plan wants hedged. Then an interest rate swap or bond futures is simpler and a TRS adds credit exposure nobody asked for. Do not look for a liability discounted at a risk-free rate: the exam's framing is the reverse, since liabilities are discounted at high-quality corporate yields while Treasury futures and swaps price off the risk-free curve, and that gap is the spread risk being tested.

The client wants to keep the upside and limit only the downside, AND listed options on the name are available. Then a protective put or a collar beats the TRS, which pays away the whole total return. Where exchange-traded options do not exist on the name (the Tundra example) or the shares are too illiquid to trade (Inwood), the keyed answer is still a cash-settled total return payer swap, even though it surrenders the upside for the swap's term.

The reallocation is large and permanent over a long horizon, where the case's rule sends the trade to the cash market and keeps derivatives for shifts that are small, temporary, levered or must be reversible.
A tax or regulatory limit in the client's jurisdiction blocks hedging the concentrated holding this way.
pitfalls: Reversing payer and receiver. The total return receiver receives the index cash flows and appreciation and pays the funding leg. To hedge an existing holding the client must be the PAYER; the receiver side just builds a second long position.

Ignoring settlement. On a physically settled single-stock swap the receiver takes delivery of the shares against the notional, so the payer gives up the stock, which defeats a client who wants to keep it. The hedge for a retained holding is a cash-settled total return PAYER swap.
Writing that a TRS eliminates counterparty credit risk. It introduces it. The advantage to cite instead is the smaller initial cash outlay for similar performance.

Dropping the income leg. Total return is price change plus dividends or coupons: in the Tundra example the stock return is [(14 x 1.01) - 14 + 0.10]/14 = 1.71%, not 1.00%, and because that beats the 0.17% six-month reference rate return the client pays the counterparty rather than receiving.

Picking the TRS for its exact replication on the unlevered mandate. Precision does not pay for 16 bps of extra cost; the answer is the ETF at 35 bps. Equally, do not carry the unlevered ranking into the levered question, because it flips.

Claiming that synthetic index exposure needs an active futures market. It does not. A TRS can be written over the counter on the desired index, which is exactly why it beats futures for a specialist or illiquid index.

cues.signal: No active futures market, or no listed contract, on the index the client wants.
cues.implication: Rules in the OTC total return swap and rules out futures. Synthetic exposure does not require an exchange-traded contract.

cues.signal: Long-held shares with a low tax basis, client will not sell, wants to keep voting rights.
cues.implication: A TRS where the client PAYS the stock's total return, cash settled. No sale, the gain is deferred, ownership and votes retained. Physical settlement and the receiver side are both wrong.

cues.signal: Worried about counterparties, wants central clearing, daily margin or exchange-traded instruments.
cues.implication: Separate the worry from the prohibition. A stated worry does not rule out the TRS: mitigate it with a Credit Support Annex, collateral and daily marking, or central clearing, which the reading says drives single-trade counterparty risk to virtually zero. In the Maestre case counterparty risk is keyed as the one risk that CAN be eliminated this way, and the same case still recommends a total return swap. Only an explicit IPS ban on OTC or uncollateralised derivatives, or a hard requirement for central clearing and daily settlement, sends you to futures or an ETF.

cues.signal: The exposure must match the index exactly, or tracking error is not tolerated.
cues.implication: Rules in the TRS, because the counterparty is obligated to deliver the index return while ETFs and futures both track imperfectly. Check the cost data before answering: precision alone lost by 16 bps in QUINCO.

cues.signal: Leverage of four times is permitted, or the account is capital constrained.
cues.implication: Futures 192 bps, TRS 201 bps, ETF 222.50 bps. The TRS beats the ETF but loses to futures. The ETF is not ineligible at 4x, it is simply dearest, because it must finance the full notional: 187.50 bps of financing (2.5% on 75% of notional) on top of its 35 bps. Its 50% regulatory margin cap, a 2x maximum, is why it is the least cash-efficient vehicle.

cues.signal: The liability discount rate includes a credit spread and the plan wants PASSIVE exposure to both rate and credit.
cues.implication: A TRS referencing a corporate bond index, economically a synthetic secured financing. Treasury futures or interest rate swaps alone hedge the rate leg and earn no credit for the credit component.

cues.signal: Small portfolio, the client doubts cell matching is worth his staff's time, costs must stay low.
cues.implication: Rules out stratified sampling and full replication. A TRS or a pooled index fund are both acceptable; the swap buys the whole index in one contract.

cues.signal: Wants exposure to high-yield loans, commercial loans or another market that is hard to access directly.
cues.implication: A customised OTC TRS, because the reading names high-yield and commercial loan investments as assets that are difficult to access directly and a customised over-the-counter contract can reach them. The ground is difficulty of access, not the size of the trade.

cues.signal: Wants to neutralise part of the equity allocation into money market like returns for six months without selling the underlying holdings.
cues.implication: Pay the equity total return and receive the floating rate on a notional equal to the slice being neutralised. The reasonableness check is that the outcome matches holding that slice in money market instruments.

cues.signal: Large, permanent strategic reallocation over a long horizon.
cues.implication: Pushes toward the cash market; derivatives are for exposure that is small, temporary, levered or must be reversible. The swap's funding spread recurs every year and its tenor has to be renewed.

instruments.name: Futures
instruments.summary: A futures contract is an exchange-traded, standardized agreement to buy or sell an underlying at a set price on a set date, cleared and marked to market daily against margin, used at Level III as an overlay to shift duration, equity beta, asset allocation or volatility exposure without trading the underlying securities. The decision it turns on is whether a standardized, liquid, cleared contract is close enough to the exposure you need, or whether the tenor, size or reference mismatch is large enough to force a customized OTC structure instead.

pros.text: A clearinghouse stands between the parties, so counterparty credit exposure is essentially eliminated. In an LDI risk list, that is the one risk choosing exchange-traded futures over OTC swaps actually removes.

Exchange-traded, standardized and cleared, so standard contracts are highly liquid and cheap to execute in size and easy to unwind. That makes futures the default for short, tactical adjustments you intend to reverse.
Capital efficient: a small initial margin controls a large notional, with leverage = (notional minus margin) / margin, so exposure can be added without funding the full position.

The exposure change happens as an overlay, leaving the underlying holdings and the external managers in place, and for a taxable investor it avoids realizing the capital gain an outright sale would trigger.
Going short is as easy as going long, with no securities borrow, which is what makes de-equitizing, hedging and duration-shortening overlays practical.

Listed prices are usable market-implied inputs: fed funds and interest-rate futures imply the market's expected path of policy rates, so a futures price can be read as a forecast rather than only traded as a hedge.

cons.text: Standardized terms create basis risk. Bond futures reference a cheapest-to-deliver bond with a conversion factor and a delivery option, and an equity beta hedge assumes a beta that is stable and correctly estimated, so a shifting beta leaves residual risk.

Government bond futures price off the sovereign curve, so they will not track a corporate bond portfolio or a liability discounted at a corporate or AA rate. That spread basis risk is a separate defect from the cheapest-to-deliver basis and survives a perfect BPV match.

Daily mark to market means variation margin is paid in cash, so an adverse move drains cash from a position that is hedged in economic terms. Even a fully invested fund running a futures overlay must hold a liquidity buffer.

Rollover risk: contracts are short-dated and must be rolled at an uncertain roll cost, quarterly for bond and equity index contracts and monthly for VIX. A long VIX futures hedge in a contango curve bleeds negative roll yield for as long as it is held.

An equity index futures hedge removes systematic market risk only. It does nothing about idiosyncratic risk, so a concentrated portfolio is still fully exposed to company-specific moves at a target beta of zero.
The hedge drifts. Portfolio value and beta both move, and the contract count has to be rebalanced to stay on target, which is ongoing cost and operational risk rather than a set-and-forget hedge.
Coverage is narrow on the fixed-income side: bond futures deliver mainly government duration and cover only part of a broad bond index, so they cannot replicate credit or securitized exposure.

whenToRecommend: The adjustment is short-horizon and tactical: a manager wants to cut duration or beta on a three-month view and expects to reverse the trade, so liquidity and easy unwind matter more than an exact tenor.

The vignette says no ISDA documentation is in place, or the mandate bars bilateral or uncleared OTC exposure. That is the categorical case for exchange trading, because a cleared swap also sits behind a CCP and so is a matter of degree rather than a different kind of exposure.

Cash has just arrived or a manager is funded but not yet invested, and cash drag needs removing: buy index futures to equitize. Contracts = cash / (futures price times multiplier) when the contract's beta is about 1, otherwise scale by beta_target / beta_futures.

A transition between markets is underway and the physical trades have not settled: short futures on the market being exited and long futures on the market being entered to hold the intended exposure in the gap.
A known future transaction needs locking in: a manager with cash arriving buys bond futures as a pre-investment hedge, and an issuer planning to borrow sells futures against rising rates.
whenNotTo: The hedge is a large, lasting, precisely matched liability hedge, such as a pension matching a 20-year liability BPV. A receive-fixed interest rate swap hits the exact tenor and notional, avoids cheapest-to-deliver basis and needs no quarterly roll. Say in the same breath that the swap substitutes swap-curve basis against a corporate-discounted liability for the futures' Treasury basis, and still carries initial and variation margin, so the swap is the better instrument rather than a clean one.

The exposure needs a non-standard size, date or underlying, for example an exact foreign-currency amount on a specific settlement date. Use a currency forward, or an FX swap to roll and resize an existing hedge.

The objective is the total return of a credit, corporate or broad bond index rather than government duration. Use a total return swap, or a sampled physical portfolio, since bond futures carry mainly government duration.

The objective is downside protection with the upside kept. Futures are symmetric and surrender the gain along with the loss, so a protective put is the answer; a collar is the cheaper version that still caps the upside at the call strike, and a put spread is cheaper still but leaves the deep downside unhedged.
The investor cannot reliably fund variation margin or has no liquidity buffer, in which case a paid-up option position or an unlevered physical holding avoids forced liquidation on a margin call.

The problem is a concentrated low-basis single stock that must be diversified without a sale. Index futures hedge only the market component. Use a total return swap paying the stock return and receiving an index return.
pitfalls: Getting the sign backwards. The formula is N_f = (BPV_target minus BPV_portfolio) / BPV_futures, so a negative answer means SELL. In a BPV-gap question the gap is liability BPV minus asset BPV, and an underhedged plan goes LONG. Wrong direction usually scores zero even with perfect arithmetic.

Ignoring the conversion factor. Futures BPV is approximately BPV of the cheapest-to-deliver divided by the conversion factor. If the vignette hands you a CTD BPV and a conversion factor, it wants that adjustment, and leaving it out shifts the contract count by the size of the factor.

Misapplying the equity formula. N_f = [(beta_target minus beta_portfolio) / beta_futures] times [V / (futures price times multiplier)]. Candidates divide by the index level instead of the full contract value, or forget to divide by the futures beta. The same divide applies to an equitization, where beta_portfolio is zero for cash.

Forgetting currency when the index futures are denominated in another currency. The beta-adjusted exposure must be converted into the contract's currency before dividing by contract value. State that the position still carries residual foreign-currency exposure, but do not reflexively prescribe a forward against it: the overlay is funded on margin rather than on the converted notional, and in an EM mandate the foreign-currency exposure is often the intended allocation.

Claiming futures remove the risks they do not. Clearing removes counterparty credit risk. Basis risk, margin and liquidity risk, roll cost, leverage and idiosyncratic risk all remain, and a hedged futures position still needs cash.

Reading 'managed futures' in an allocation or alternatives vignette as this instrument. There it is a trend-following hedge fund strategy held as an equity-risk mitigator for its crisis alpha, not a duration or beta overlay.

cues.signal: The vignette says no ISDA is in place, or that the mandate bars bilateral or uncleared OTC exposure.
cues.implication: Rules out forwards and uncleared swaps, rules in exchange-traded futures and listed options. A bare mention of counterparty concern is weaker than it looks: a standard interest rate swap is centrally cleared and collateralized, so the difference from futures there is degree, not kind, and a swap can still be the answer.

cues.signal: Words like tactical, temporary, three-month view, until the physical portfolio is rebalanced, or until the new manager is funded.
cues.implication: Futures over swaps. Short horizon plus easy unwind is exactly the futures case, and the roll cost barely bites over one or two contract cycles.

cues.signal: Match the liability duration precisely, a named long tenor, avoid rolling every quarter, or a pension closing a funded-status gap for good.
cues.implication: A receive-fixed interest rate swap wins. Exact tenor and notional, no cheapest-to-deliver basis, no quarterly roll. Futures remain defensible on liquidity and clearing, so argue both sides rather than declaring the swap flawless.

cues.signal: A cheapest-to-deliver BPV and a conversion factor are given.
cues.implication: A contract count is being asked for, not a swap notional, and the conversion factor must be used: futures BPV = CTD BPV / conversion factor. The factor tells you the futures arithmetic is wanted here; it is not by itself a signal that futures are the recommended instrument.

cues.signal: A futures price, a contract multiplier, a portfolio beta and a target beta are given.
cues.implication: Equity beta hedge ratio. Sign comes from target minus current beta, and target beta zero is the full hedge. Answer in whole contracts with the direction stated.

cues.signal: Liability BPV exceeds asset BPV, or the manager expects rates to fall and wants more interest-rate sensitivity.
cues.implication: Buy, that is go LONG, bond futures to add BPV. The mirror case, assets over-hedged relative to liabilities or a rate-rise view, is SHORT.

cues.signal: Cash sitting uninvested, cash drag quantified in basis points, or a mandate funded ahead of deployment.
cues.implication: Equitize with long index futures. Contracts = cash / (futures price times multiplier) when the contract's beta is about 1; when a futures beta is supplied, scale by beta_target / beta_futures. Reverse it, short index futures against an equity holding, creates synthetic cash and earns roughly the risk-free rate without selling stock.

cues.signal: Keep the external managers, do not disturb the underlying holdings, or do not realize capital gains.
cues.implication: An overlay answer, futures or swaps, rather than physical trading. For a multi-manager fund left short a region or a duration bucket, name it a completion overlay.

cues.signal: The VIX curve is in contango and the proposed tail hedge is long VIX futures.
cues.implication: Credit the hedge for rising when volatility spikes, then name negative roll yield as a persistent drag. A long variance swap is the cleaner crash hedge because it has no roll and pays on realized variance, which is convex in volatility. Selling options on VIX futures is an income trade, not a hedge: the gain is capped at the premium just when payoff is needed.

cues.signal: A fed funds futures price such as 98.33 alongside the current policy rate.
cues.implication: Implied rate = 100 minus price. Then set expected rate = P(move) times the post-move rate plus the complement times the current rate and solve for P. The question is about inferring market expectations from derivative prices, not about hedging.

cues.signal: The fund is described as fully invested with no cash reserve, and an overlay is being proposed.
cues.implication: Flag variation margin. Daily settlement can force an asset sale at the worst moment, so the recommendation must come with a liquidity buffer. This is a standard mark-grabbing point.

cues.signal: The position being hedged is one stock or a handful of names, and a beta hedge is proposed.
cues.implication: Systematic risk goes, idiosyncratic risk stays. Say so explicitly, and if the objective is actually diversification without a sale, redirect to a total return swap.

cues.signal: The index futures are quoted in a different currency from the portfolio, for example BRL contracts against a USD exposure.
cues.implication: Convert the beta-adjusted exposure into the contract currency before dividing by contract value, and state that the position leaves residual currency exposure. Whether to hedge that exposure is a separate decision the vignette has to ask for.

cues.signal: The liabilities are discounted at a corporate or AA rate while the hedge instrument is a Treasury future.
cues.implication: Spread basis risk, not counterparty risk, is the live issue. The hedge tracks the government curve and the liability does not, so a parallel-shift hedge can still move the funded ratio.

instruments.name: Forwards
instruments.summary: An over-the-counter contract to buy or sell an asset, a currency or a rate at a price agreed today for one settlement date, with no daily settlement. The decision it turns on is customization against counterparty risk and liquidity: take an exact notional and date and accept bilateral credit exposure, or take a listed future's standard size, fixed expiry and clearinghouse.

pros.text: Customizable to the exact notional, currency and date of the exposure, so the hedge leaves no size or maturity residual.
No daily settlement, so no variation margin and no daily margin calls. Cash demands arrive at maturity or at each roll date, which a client with a thin liquidity buffer can plan around.
No upfront premium: a full forward hedge locks the rate at zero initial cost, where an option hedge has to be paid for.
The default currency hedging tool: sell a long foreign-currency exposure forward, then roll it with an FX swap, which is also how the hedge ratio is resized.

Pricing is mechanical, not a forecast. Covered interest rate parity fixes the forward premium or discount at the interest-rate differential, so the carry on the contract being written is known when it is struck, and a fully hedged foreign risk-free (money market) investment earns the domestic risk-free rate.
Available on far more currency pairs, sizes and maturities than listed currency futures, which is why currency hedges are run with forwards and FX swaps rather than exchange-traded contracts.
Non-deliverable forwards extend forward hedging to currencies that are not convertible or deliverable, cash settling the difference between the contracted rate and spot in a convertible currency.

cons.text: Bilateral counterparty credit risk: performance depends on the dealer, with no clearinghouse between the parties. Collateral and central clearing mitigate it and a listed future largely removes it, but a forward does not.

Less liquid than futures for standardized exposures: for a duration or equity-beta overlay the listed bond and index futures are the deep venue, so an exposure that will be resized or exited repeatedly belongs there. This does not carry over to currency, where forwards and FX swaps are the venue.
The payoff is symmetric, so a full forward hedge gives up all favorable currency movement along with the downside. There is no participation in appreciation.

Hedging a higher-yielding foreign currency, the one trading at a forward discount, costs roll yield: the hedge sells below spot and gives up the rate differential at every roll. Each roll is also struck at the then-prevailing differential, so the cost of a multi-period hedging program is not locked at inception.

One maturity and one fixed notional, so the hedge has to be rolled and resized. As the underlying asset value moves, a static hedge drifts off target: a rising asset is under-hedged, a falling one over-hedged.

Hedges only the exposure written into the contract. An FX forward does nothing about the asset's duration, spread or equity risk, which is why a foreign bond needs the forward for currency plus bond futures or a swap for duration.

whenToRecommend: The exposure is a known amount on a known date, for example a foreign-currency receipt in seven months, and a standardized contract would leave an unhedged residual and an expiry mismatch.
A long foreign-currency asset exposure has to be brought to the hedge ratio the IPS specifies: sell the foreign currency forward, then roll and resize with FX swaps.
The client cannot support daily variation margin, or the vignette flags the operational burden of daily margining. Still say that cash is needed at each roll date when the hedge is out of the money.
The currency faces capital controls or is not deliverable, so the hedge has to be a non-deliverable forward, or a proxy hedge in a correlated liquid currency with basis risk accepted.
One rate or price has to be locked for a single date and amount, or the exposure change is tailored or longer dated. A swap's series of exchanges is more machinery than a one-date exposure needs.
whenNotTo: The mandate prohibits OTC or uncleared instruments: use exchange-traded futures and accept standardized sizes, fixed expiries, basis risk and daily margin.
