It is the minimum-variance position only where that covariance is zero or positive; where the correlation is negative the unhedged position can be the less volatile one and h* falls below 1.

Separates the currency decision from the asset decision. Because the domestic-currency return decomposes into the asset return and the currency return, a manager can keep a foreign asset they like and hedge away a currency they do not.

A forward hedge needs no upfront premium, unlike buying a currency option. It is not costless, though: where the foreign currency is at a forward discount the negative roll yield is realized in cash at every roll (see the roll-cost con below), margin or collateral may still be posted, and all of the currency upside is surrendered.

With no currency view and roughly zero expected currency return, there is no expected-return argument for carrying the exposure. Theory does not pin down a single best hedge ratio, so a risk reducer can anchor to full hedging, which the notes label the minimum-risk default, or to 50% as the regret-minimizing compromise that avoids both extremes.
The hedge ratio is adjustable without touching the underlying assets. An FX swap rolls a maturing forward to a new date and resizes the notional in the same trade.

The exposure can be carved out to a currency overlay mandate benchmarked to the strategic hedge ratio, either as a pure hedging mandate that keeps the hedge on target or as an active mandate that is paid for currency views.

cons.text: A full hedge gives up currency diversification as well as currency upside. Currencies are imperfectly correlated, so a multi-currency portfolio's aggregate currency risk is less than the sum of its single-currency exposures, and hedging each one separately throws that netting away.
It does not protect the asset. A fully hedged position still carries the asset's entire local-currency volatility, because the hedge fixes the exchange rate, not the price.

Quantity risk forces ongoing rebalancing. A forward fixes a rate on a fixed notional while the asset value moves, so a rise leaves the position under-hedged and a fall over-hedged. How tightly you rebalance is a trade-off: tighter triggers hold the hedge ratio near target and cut tracking error against the benchmark, but cost more in transactions. Residual exposure never disappears, so the realistic goal is a target level of currency risk consistent with the IPS, not zero.

Hedging the higher-yielding currency is expensive. If the foreign currency carries the higher interest rate it trades at a forward discount, so each roll sells it below spot and the hedge bleeds roughly the interest differential, whatever the spot rate does.
Where no exact instrument exists the hedge is a cross hedge in a correlated currency, which leaves basis risk because the hedge and the exposure do not move one for one.

Forwards, FX swaps and non-deliverable forwards are OTC and bilateral, so they carry counterparty credit exposure that centrally cleared, exchange-traded currency futures effectively remove. The cash trade-off runs the other way: futures impose initial and daily variation margin, while a forward has no daily settlement and posts collateral only where a credit support annex requires it. NDF credit risk sits between the two, because only the net difference is ever exchanged.

whenToRecommend: The foreign holdings are BONDS. The local-currency return is relatively stable, so the currency can be the dominant source of domestic-currency risk, and a high hedge ratio is the standard answer.
The investor has a short horizon or low risk tolerance and cannot afford to wait out a currency swing on the argument that it will mean-revert.
A large proportion of the portfolio sits in foreign assets, or the asset-currency correlation is high, so the currency contributes heavily to total portfolio risk.

Hedging is cheap because the foreign currency is the LOWER-yielding one and so trades at a forward premium. Selling it forward sells it above spot, and the roll earns rather than costs, which argues for a higher hedge ratio.

The IPS sets a benchmark hedge ratio and a permitted band and the position has drifted outside it, or the asset value has moved so the existing hedge notional is off target. These are two different jobs: rebalance with an FX swap if the forward is maturing, since unequal legs resize it in the same trade, or with an additional outright forward to the existing settlement date if it is not.
whenNotTo: The horizon is long and risk tolerance is high, and the manager accepts that currency effects largely wash out over that horizon. Run a lower strategic hedge ratio or leave the exposure open.

The exposure is foreign EQUITY, whose own volatility dwarfs the currency's, and in some markets equity and currency returns are negatively correlated, giving a natural partial hedge. Hedge equities far less fully than bonds.

The foreign currency is the HIGHER-yielding one, so it trades at a forward discount and every roll sells it below spot. Consider a lower hedge ratio, an out-of-the-money option, or a SHORT risk reversal rather than a full forward hedge.

The client wants to keep the gain if the currency appreciates. A forward surrenders all of it, so buy a put, or fund the put by writing an out-of-the-money call, which is a SHORT risk reversal, and accept the cap on the favorable side.

The currency is not freely deliverable or is subject to capital controls, so a plain forward is unavailable. Use a non-deliverable forward, or cross hedge in a correlated major currency and accept basis risk.

The position is a deliberate long in a high-yielding currency funded by a low-yielding one. Hedging it away removes exactly the carry the trade is being paid for, so size and tail-limit the position instead of hedging it.
pitfalls: Adding the asset and currency returns. R_DC = (1 + R_FC)(1 + R_FX) - 1 is multiplicative, so include the cross product: 8% and 3% give 11.24%, not 11%.
Dropping the covariance term from the risk formula. Use σ²(R_DC) ≈ σ²(R_FC) + σ²(R_FX) + 2ρ(R_FC,R_FX)σ(R_FC)σ(R_FX), and remember a fully hedged position still leaves σ(R_FC).

Capping the minimum-variance hedge ratio between 0 and 1. The 0 to 100% range is a statement about STRATEGIC hedge ratios in practice; h* is a regression beta, so it exceeds 1 only when ρ × σ(R_DC)/σ(R_FX) > 1, which needs the asset's domestic-currency return to be both positively correlated with the currency AND more volatile than it. Correlation alone is not enough: ρ 0.90 with σ_DC 5% and σ_FX 10% gives h* = 0.45, a partial hedge. It goes negative whenever the correlation is negative.
Putting σ(R_FC) in the numerator of h*. The regression is the asset's DOMESTIC-currency return on the currency return: h* = ρ(R_DC, R_FX) × σ(R_DC)/σ(R_FX).

Getting the roll-yield sign backwards. Selling a forward-DISCOUNT currency (the higher-yielding one) forward sells it below spot, so the hedge COSTS roughly the interest differential; selling a forward-PREMIUM currency (the lower-yielding one) forward sells it above spot and EARNS roll yield. WARNING, your own reading notes for Currency Management have this INVERTED in six places: the roll-yield paragraph, both worked examples, the LOS 5 and 6 exam-focus line, the quick-reference card and self-test Q7. The curriculum rule, and the way the question bank grades it, is that positive roll yield comes from BUYING at a forward discount or SELLING at a forward premium. Trust this card over those six passages, and get the notes fixed.

Calling a risen foreign asset over-hedged. The hedge notional is fixed, so an asset that has gained value has outgrown it and is UNDER-hedged, and you sell additional forward. A fall is what leaves it over-hedged.

cues.signal: The foreign holdings are fixed income, or the vignette stresses that the local-currency return is stable while the currency is volatile.
cues.implication: Currency is the dominant share of domestic-currency risk, so argue a HIGH hedge ratio. If the same portfolio also holds foreign equity, argue a lower ratio on that sleeve in the same answer, because equity volatility dwarfs the currency's.

cues.signal: The forward rate on the foreign currency is quoted BELOW spot, or the foreign currency is named as the higher-interest-rate one.
cues.implication: Forward discount, so selling it forward locks in a rate below spot and the hedge loses roughly the interest differential on every roll. High hedging cost argues for a LOWER hedge ratio, or an out-of-the-money option or short risk reversal instead of a full forward. Reverse the whole argument if the forward is above spot.

cues.signal: The IPS or the trustees limit the hedging tools permitted, or bar OTC derivatives.
cues.implication: The IPS sets the tools permitted as well as the benchmark hedge ratio and the discretionary band, so check it before recommending an instrument. If OTC is barred, short exchange-traded currency futures and concede that standard contract sizes and expiry dates make the notional less precise. Do not argue that a central-clearing requirement rules out NDFs: NDFs are commonly cleared or collateralized.

cues.signal: The IPS states a benchmark hedge ratio with a permitted range around it.
cues.implication: The question is about discretion inside the band, not whether to hedge at all. The overlay is benchmarked to that strategic hedge ratio, not to 0% and not to 100%, so performance is measured relative to it and any recommendation has to stay inside the stated range.

cues.signal: The foreign asset has risen or fallen in value since the hedge was placed, or the existing forward is about to mature.
cues.implication: Two different jobs, so read which one fired. If the forward is MATURING, roll it with an FX SWAP, a spot transaction plus an offsetting forward, and resize in the same trade by making the legs unequal. If the forward is still outstanding and only the asset value has moved, leave it in place and trade an additional OUTRIGHT forward to that same settlement date: sell more forward if the asset has risen, buy some back if it has fallen. The LOS names forward contracts AND FX swaps, so say which one and why.

cues.signal: The client wants protection against depreciation but refuses to give up the gain if the currency appreciates.
cues.implication: Rules out a forward and an FX swap entirely, because both surrender the whole upside. Buy an out-of-the-money put on the foreign currency; if the premium is also objected to, fund it by writing an out-of-the-money call, which is a SHORT risk reversal, or use a put spread, accepting a cap on the favorable side or an incomplete floor. Name the side: in FX a long call plus a short put is the LONG risk reversal, so the hedger's collar is the short one.

cues.signal: The currency is non-deliverable, subject to capital controls, or no liquid forward is quoted in it.
cues.implication: Rules out a deliverable forward. Use a non-deliverable forward, which cash settles the difference between the contracted forward rate and the spot fixing in the NON-CONTROLLED, freely convertible currency of the pair, conventionally USD, with the restricted currency never delivered. Or cross hedge with a correlated liquid currency sized by the regression beta. Both leave basis risk, and that basis tends to widen in exactly the crisis the hedge was bought for. Two NDF-specific points worth a mark: the NDF rate can diverge from the onshore rate, and because capital controls break cross-border arbitrage, NDF pricing need not satisfy covered interest parity.

cues.signal: The portfolio holds many small exposures across numerous currencies and the mandate objects to the cost of hedging each one.
cues.implication: Macro hedge: one derivative on a currency basket or index taken against the portfolio's broad currency risk. Cheaper and simpler to administer than hedging currency by currency, but less precise, since it addresses aggregate exposure rather than any single pair.

cues.signal: The vignette supplies a correlation between the asset's domestic-currency return and the currency return, plus the two standard deviations.
cues.implication: It wants the minimum-variance hedge ratio h* = ρ × σ(R_DC)/σ(R_FX), not a full hedge. Report it as the percentage of exposure to sell forward and state that it hedges the currency plus the part of asset risk correlated with the currency. With ρ 0.60, σ_DC 10% and σ_FX 8%, h* is 75%.

cues.signal: The phrase 'hedge ratio' appears in a pension, LDI or liability context rather than a currency one.
cues.implication: That is the LIABILITY rate hedge ratio, how much of the liability's interest-rate risk is hedged, not a currency hedge ratio. Different instruments (interest-rate swaps, futures, swaptions) and different arithmetic (basis point value), so do not reach for forwards, FX swaps or roll yield.

instruments.name: Carry Trade
instruments.summary: A carry trade borrows (shorts) a low-yield funding currency and invests (longs) a high-yield currency, earning the interest rate differential. The decision it turns on is whether the differential pays enough to hold unhedged spot risk in a currency that can crash, because hedging that risk removes the carry.

pros.text: It earns the rate differential without needing the high-yield currency to appreciate. If spot is unchanged the position collects the differential, and it stays profitable until the high-yield currency depreciates by more than that differential.

It exploits a documented empirical failure rather than a hunch. UIP says the high-yield currency should depreciate by the differential, but at short horizons high-yield currencies tend to hold up or appreciate, so the trade has historically paid.

Carry is one of the few persistent sources of active currency return, alongside value, momentum and the volatility risk premium, and it is the one that trades the rate differential rather than valuation, trend or implied volatility.
The opportunity set is widest where rate dispersion is widest. Funding at 1% into an emerging market currency yielding 9% is an 8% carry, and the notes pair that wider carry with the worse tail.

It can be expressed in the forward market instead of by borrowing, by buying the currency at a forward discount (the high-yield one) and selling the currency at a forward premium (the low-yield one), which is trading the forward rate bias. If spot does not move, the buyer of the forward-discount currency collects the forward points, and the trade can be run as an overlay without disturbing the underlying asset managers.

cons.text: The payoff is negatively skewed: steady earnings in calm markets, then a sharp loss when the high-yield currency crashes in a risk-off episode. The phrase in the notes is picking up nickels in front of a steamroller.

One devaluation erases years of carry. The notes' own illustration funds at 1% into a 9% currency for an 8% carry, then a 25% devaluation leaves roughly minus 17%, which undoes about three years of accumulated carry. Timing makes it worse: the move arrives in weeks, when barely any of that 8% has accrued, so the realised loss is nearer the whole 25%.

It protects against nothing and is unhedged by construction. By covered interest rate parity a foreign money market investment with the currency sold forward just earns the domestic rate, so the carry exists only as payment for holding the spot risk.

Volatility and Sharpe ratios flatter it, because the return distribution is negatively skewed and fat-tailed. Risk control has to come from conservative position sizing, stop-losses and explicit tail-risk limits rather than from the Sharpe ratio.

Diversifying across several high-yield currencies fails in the one event that matters. Contagion makes emerging market currencies crash together, so the positions share a common risk-off factor rather than carrying independent risks.

The differential is fixed only for the term of the two legs. Run as rolling short-dated positions, which is the usual implementation, a hike in the funding currency or a cut in the investment currency compresses it at the next roll while the full spot exposure stays in place. Lengthening the legs, or using a single dated forward, fixes the forward points for that horizon but leaves the spot risk untouched; hedging the spot leg with an offsetting forward is the one move that removes the risk, and it removes the carry with it. Funded and forward-based positions also embed leverage, which magnifies a forced unwind.

whenToRecommend: The vignette describes calm markets, low and stable FX volatility, a wide rate differential and no imminent policy turn in the funding currency.
The IPS permits active currency management within discretionary bands, or the account runs a separate currency overlay benchmarked to the strategic hedge ratio.
The horizon of the view is short. UIP fails at short horizons, so a carry view is defensible over months, while PPP is the anchor for a multi-year forecast.
The investor has real tail-risk capacity: no near-term forced liquidation, a position small relative to total assets, and position limits, stop-losses or bought option protection already specified.
whenNotTo: The IPS prohibits speculative or unhedged currency exposure, or the investor is short-horizon or liability-driven. Do not put the trade on. There is no hedged version of it, because selling the high-yield currency forward surrenders the differential and leaves only the domestic rate. If the account already holds the high-yield currency through its foreign assets, that exposure is a hedging decision, not a carry trade.
Risk-off conditions: FX volatility rising, credit spreads widening, a flight to quality. This is the regime in which carry unwinds, so cut the position rather than add to it.
The manager's view is on the size of the move rather than its direction. Trade FX volatility with options, a straddle or a strangle, not carry.

The investment currency is non-convertible or under capital controls. The position can only be expressed through non-deliverable forwards, which add basis risk between the NDF and onshore rates, counterparty risk and poor liquidity.

The role being filled is diversification or crisis protection. Carry loses exactly when risk assets lose, so it is not a hedge. Use duration in high-quality government bonds, or a protective put, for that job.
The investor wants the yield pickup but cannot accept the left tail. Size the position down and buy a put on the high-yield currency, accepting lower expected carry in exchange for a floor.
pitfalls: Writing the legs backwards. Long and invest the HIGH-yield currency, short and borrow the LOW-yield currency. An essay answer has to name both legs to earn the mark.
Saying the trade relies on UIP. It is a bet against UIP. CIP is an arbitrage identity and holds; UIP is only a theory, and its short-horizon failure is the entire source of the return.

Getting the return arithmetic wrong. The trade loses only if the high-yield currency depreciates by MORE than the differential, so a 4% carry survives up to 4% of depreciation, and the differential has to be scaled to the holding period (an annualised 4% carry is about 1% over three months) while the spot move is not annualised.

Confusing currency carry with repo carry. In a yield curve vignette, carry means buying a higher-yielding bond financed at a lower repo rate under a static upward-sloping curve, which is a leverage decision, not a currency one.

Trying to make the trade safe by hedging it. Selling the high-yield currency forward gives up about the differential, leaving only the domestic rate, so the carry and a forward hedge cannot coexist. A bought put floors the tail while surrendering only the premium rather than the whole differential, so some carry survives, but expected carry is lower, not unchanged. Name position sizing, stop-losses and tail-risk limits as the rest of the risk control, and add that a stop can gap through in a crash, which is why bought protection is the only hard floor.

Your own reading notes for LOS 5 and 6 of the currency reading state the roll-yield sign BACKWARDS, in the summary bullet, both worked examples, the exam-focus line and self-test question 7. The correct sign, which your flashcards and the question bank both carry: hedging means SELLING the currency forward, so hedging a forward-DISCOUNT (high-yield) currency COSTS roughly the differential (negative roll yield), and hedging a forward-PREMIUM (low-yield) currency EARNS it. The carry trader, who buys the forward-discount currency, is on the collecting side.

cues.signal: Two money market rates are given and the vignette says the exchange rate is expected to be unchanged, or asks for the return if spot holds.
cues.implication: Carry trade. The return is approximately the differential, the investment rate minus the funding rate, scaled to the holding period. Do not apply UIP and depreciate the high-yield currency, which would hand back the whole pickup. If several pairs are given, the choice rule is both screens together: the widest yield spread AND the lowest implied volatility among the candidate pairs. Borrow the lowest-yield currency, invest in the highest-yield one, and name the volatility screen in the justification.

cues.signal: The manager believes the high-yield currency will not depreciate as much as the forward rate implies, or the vignette names the forward rate bias.
cues.implication: The same trade in forward market language: buy the currency trading at a forward discount, which is the high-yield one, and sell the currency at a forward premium, which is the low-yield one. Recommend carry and say explicitly that it is a bet against UIP.

cues.signal: A foreign money market position, or a foreign bond's yield pickup, is fully hedged back to the domestic currency, and the question asks where the yield advantage went or what the hedge costs.
cues.implication: Covered interest rate parity. The high-yield foreign currency trades at a forward discount, so selling it forward means selling below spot: the hedge gives up roughly the differential (negative roll yield). For a foreign MONEY MARKET position that makes the hedged return exactly the domestic rate. For a foreign BOND the hedge removes only the short-rate differential, leaving the domestic cash rate plus whatever the bond earns above foreign cash: term premium, credit spread, price change. What vanishes is the money-market yield advantage, not the bond's excess return. Capturing the money-market pickup requires leaving the currency unhedged, which is the carry trade.

cues.signal: A currency program shows several years of steady returns, low volatility and a high Sharpe ratio.
cues.implication: The question is setting up a skew critique. Answer on negative skew and tail risk, not on the reported Sharpe. Credit strategies are flagged for the same trap, so the cue can appear outside the currency reading.

cues.signal: A high-yielding emerging market currency, or several EM carry positions presented as a diversified book.
cues.implication: EM carry: the widest carry and the worst tail. Contagion crashes those currencies together, so spreading the trade across pairs is not risk control. Answer with conservative sizing, explicit tail-risk limits, and bought puts rather than forwards where a floor is required.

cues.signal: The investment currency is non-convertible or under capital controls.
cues.implication: The trade and any hedge can only go through non-deliverable forwards, so an IPS that bars counterparty exposure or illiquid instruments rules it out altogether rather than merely sizing it down.

cues.signal: The IPS sets a strategic hedge ratio with discretionary bands, and the question asks where an active currency view belongs.
cues.implication: Carry is taken inside those bands, or as a separate overlay mandate benchmarked to the strategic hedge ratio and judged on information ratio against it. It is not a reason to abandon the strategic ratio.

cues.signal: Risk-off language: spreads widening, a flight to quality, FX volatility spiking, forced deleveraging.
cues.implication: This is the unwind episode. Recommend reducing or exiting the carry.

cues.signal: The vignette describes a manager's currency approach and asks which style it is, or asks the candidate to compare the active styles.
cues.implication: The command word in the official LOS (currency_management_an_introduction.d) is COMPARE, so give the bet each style places, not just the label: carry trades the rate differential; fundamentals trades valuation via PPP and flows; technical trades trend and momentum while ignoring fundamentals; volatility trades implied against realised volatility with FX options.

cues.signal: A fixed income vignette with an upward-sloping curve, a view that the curve will stay STATIC or UNCHANGED (so the forwards are NOT realized), and the word carry.
cues.implication: Fixed income carry, not currency carry. Wrong instrument, wrong answer: go to the repo_leverage entry for the mechanics. Keep the two 'agree with the market' cases apart, because the exam separates them: a static-curve view rewards added duration, rolldown and repo carry, but if the vignette instead says rates will evolve as the forwards imply, the forwards ARE realized, every bond earns the same horizon return, and the answer is a neutral benchmark-matching posture, not carry.
